title: Historic Deal Positions FIA World Endurance Championship for Record Decade of Growth as the Sport Enters its Golden Age
summary: Sport news The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the global governing body for motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations worldwide, and the Automobile Club de l’Ouest (ACO), the founder and organiser of the 24 Hours of Le Mans, have today announced a major deal for the FIA World Endurance Championship (FIA WEC), securing another decade of growth.   The landmark agreement, which comes during a period of unprecedented growth for the championship, will ensure a common ambition to expand the partnership and drive its commercial success. It will run from the end of 2027, when the current agreement expires, to the end of 2037.    Under the extended partnership agreement, all regulatory processes will be overseen by FIA Working Groups, the FIA Endurance Commission, and will require the final approval of the FIA World Motor Sport Council. The homologation process has also been streamlined, with the FIA and ACO overseeing the homologation of all cars competing in the Hypercar class.   The renewed partnership will also deliver significantly increased branding for the FIA. This includes enhanced branding prominently displayed across key areas including parc fermé, the podium and the Safety Cars, as well as across broadcast coverage.   With an expanding fanbase, a wider pool of competitors, and a global calendar of iconic events, the championship is stronger than ever. Since its inception in 2012, it has set the global standard for long-distance circuit racing. Following the introduction of the Hypercar regulations in 2021, interest in the championship from motor sport fans and from the automotive world has surged.    FIA WEC’s trackside audience has grown 8% so far in 2026, with millions of fans following the championship globally. The fanbase for the championship is also evolving. This year, 44% of attendees are aged 34 or younger, while 40% are attending an FIA WEC event for the first time. The championship has secured the long-term loyalty of its existing fanbase, while building the next generation of endurance racing fans.   Eight of the world’s leading auto-manufacturers currently compete in Hypercar, the top category of FIA WEC. Following the addition of the LMGT3 class in 2024, the championship now counts no fewer than 14 marques in total on the starting grid. Two more giants of the automotive industry – Ford and McLaren – are set to join the Hypercar ranks in 2027.   For over 100 years, endurance racing has served as a proven testbed for technologies that transfer from track to road. This renewed agreement creates a solid framework for advancing hydrogen powertrains in competition, providing a clear pathway toward more sustainable transport and mobility.    It will also deliver a more unified technical framework that defines top-level endurance racing Hypercars competing both in the FIA WEC and IMSA in North America, which will be introduced from 2030.  The new framework will provide greater cost-efficiency for manufacturers to compete in endurance racing championships and events globally, boosting potential participation and increasing the spectacle for motor sport fans.   With interest in FIA WEC at levels never seen before, the championship is positioned for continued growth and success over the coming decade. This new deal offers the solid foundation needed to secure its future, marking a milestone moment in the history of FIA WEC.    Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA , said:  “This is not simply an agreement, it is a vital step forward for racing that will secure the future of the FIA World Endurance Championship for years to come.     “This is a deal built for the future, a deal of the century, one that strengthens the collaboration between the FIA and ACO, a relationship that dates back over 120 years, and sets the championship up for a decade of record growth that will deliver real benefits to fans, drivers, teams and manufacturers.     “It has been an honour to play a part in the collaboration that has helped usher in this golden age of endurance racing. I look forward to continuing our work alongside President Pierre Fillon and his team as we build on this momentum and shape an even stronger future.”     Pierre Fillon, President of the Automobile Club de l'Ouest , said: “ We are delighted to see the agreement between the FIA and the ACO extended, reinforcing the strong and long-standing relationship that has been at the heart of the FIA World Endurance Championship since its creation in 2012. This partnership has been built on trust, shared ambition, and a common commitment to the development of endurance racing.      “Together, the FIA and the ACO have created a solid foundation for the continued success and international growth of the championship, and we look forward to writing the next chapter of this remarkable collaboration. Finally, I would like to thank FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem for the great relationship we have built.”      Alberto Villarreal, General Manager at the FIA , said:  “The FIA World Endurance Championship is stronger and more popular than it has ever been before, with a growing and evolving fanbase, and an impressive roster of top-tier global auto-manufacturers.      “The agreement announced today underlines the investment in the championship from both the FIA and the ACO, and our commitment to continue bringing the sport to new audiences. It is a pivotal moment in the history of FIA WEC, and provides the foundation and stability needed for the championship’s ongoing success.”      Frédéric Lequien, CEO of the Le Mans Endurance Management, the promoter for the FIA World Endurance Championship , said:  “This agreement comes at an exciting time for the FIA World Endurance Championship. The championship is experiencing exceptional momentum, with growing engagement from manufacturers, teams, partners, media, and fans around the world. The extension provides a strong framework to build on this growth, further strengthen the global appeal of the WEC and continue to deliver a world-class championship at the forefront of endurance racing. We are looking forward to an ambitious and exciting future for the FIA WEC.”     -   Notes to Editors     The renewed agreement between the FIA and the ACO follows three other significant long-term agreement announcements since July 2025:      FIA and Formula E sign landmark extension to power Formula E World Championship for another 10 years, announced in July 2025 –  information here        Multi-year Concorde Governance Agreement between the FIA, Formula 1 Group and all 11 race teams, announced in December 2025 –  information here        “Deal of the Century” for FIA World and European Rally Championships in July 2026 –  information here         These announcements form part of the FIA’s strategic investment in the future of motor sport, as it continues its mission to grow participation in the sport and provide a safe and accessible platform for all.      The FIA has seen a radical transformation since 2021, and earlier this year  announced  that it had delivered its strongest set of financial results in a decade in 2025, with an operating profit of €6.7m. It also reported an exceptional gain of €20m through the Formula E contract extension.    About the FIA  The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.   Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 246 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. It develops and enforces regulations for motor sport, including six FIA World Championships, to ensure worldwide competitions are safe and fair for all.    About the ACO   Founded in 1906, the Automobile Club de l’Ouest (ACO) is the creator and organiser of major motorsport events: the first Grand Prix in history in 1906, followed by the 24 Hours of Le Mans starting in 1923. The ACO has also been the organiser and promoter of the FIA World Endurance Championship (FIA WEC) since 2012 and the creator of continental series: the European Le Mans Series (2004) and the Asian Le Mans Series (2013). The ACO organises the 24 Hours of Le Mans Motorcycle Race, the 24 Hours of Le Mans Karting, the 24 Hours of Le Mans Truck Race, and the French Motorcycle Grand Prix on its Le Mans circuits…   The 24 Hours of Le Mans serves as a true technological laboratory focused on automotive innovation. It is in this spirit that the ACO continues to evolve. Sustainable mobility - embodied in particular by MissionH24, which aims to introduce hydrogen to the 24 Hours of Le Mans - is a key objective for the ACO.   Since 2024, the ACO has held the FIA’s 3-star environmental accreditation and is ISO 20121 certified, the benchmark for responsible event management. In September 2024, the 24 Hours of Le Mans circuit was also voted “France’s Favourite Monument.”    About FIA WEC  The FIA World Endurance Championship (FIA WEC), created in 2012 by the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA) and the Automobile Club de l’Ouest (ACO), represents the undisputed pinnacle of the long-distance discipline.   Bringing together the world’s leading manufacturers, biggest brands, top drivers and most successful teams, FIA WEC races around the globe, pushing the limits of speed, performance and durability while encouraging ever-greater feats of strategic skill. If the fast and fearless drivers are the heroes, then the cars are the stars, from their cutting-edge technology to their dynamic design. And then, of course, there is the sound of the engines – that uncompromising, unadulterated roar.   The cornerstone of the calendar is the iconic 24 Hours of Le Mans, an event born in 1923 that continues to serve as the ultimate test for manufacturers seeking to prove their mettle – but every race has its own character, challenges and pitfalls. As a series with a proud history, a compelling present and a thrilling future, FIA WEC remains endurance racing’s global benchmark, continuously setting the standard in the sport and inspiring generations to come. title: FIA Asia Pacific Congress to Bring Member Clubs Together in the Philippines to Advance Mobility and Motor Sport Across the Region
summary: Members news    The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the global governing body for motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations worldwide, will be hosted by the Automobile Association Philippines (AAP) in Boracay in the Philippines for its Asia Pacific Congress next week, bringing together FIA Member Clubs from across the region.  From 29 September to 1 October, 120 delegates from Member Clubs across Asia and the Pacific, will unite in Boracay for three days of collaboration, innovation and knowledge sharing. Throughout the week, attendees will discuss priorities to advance safe and sustainable mobility for road users and drive greater motor sport accessibility.  The Asia-Pacific region is one of the FIA's most diverse and dynamic, spanning some of the world's fastest-growing mobility markets and an expanding motor sport community. The Congress will provide Member Clubs with an opportunity to share expertise and develop practical solutions which respond to the specific needs of their members and communities.  Across mobility, discussions will focus on road safety, innovation, sustainable and accessible transport, tourism and the changing needs of road users, building on the FIA's work to support Clubs in delivering meaningful impact at a national and regional level.  Motor sport sessions will explore opportunities to increase participation, strengthen grassroots competition and create more accessible pathways into the sport, supporting the FIA's ambition to make motor sport more affordable and accessible around the world.  The programme will also showcase the work and innovation of FIA Member Clubs across Asia-Pacific, providing a platform to share successful initiatives which can be adapted and scaled across the region.   H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, said:   "The Asia-Pacific region is central to the future of both mobility and motor sport, and our Member Clubs are at the heart of that progress.   From improving road safety and embracing innovation to creating new opportunities for people to participate in motor sport, our Clubs are delivering real impact for their communities.    "The FIA Asia Pacific Congress gives us an important opportunity to bring that expertise together, share ideas and strengthen collaboration across one of the most diverse and dynamic regions in our Federation.    "I thank our hosts the Automobile Association Philippines, and President Joe Ferreria, for welcoming the FIA family to Boracay and look forward to another productive Congress."    FIA Region II President and President of host club the Automobile Association Philippines, Augustus ‘Joe’ Ferreria said:   "The strength of this region comes from the diversity, knowledge and ambition of our Member Clubs. Bringing our community together in the Philippines gives us the opportunity to learn from one another, identify shared challenges and develop solutions that can support Clubs across the region.    "The Asia Pacific Congress is an important moment for us to build on the progress already being made and ensure our Clubs have the tools, knowledge and connections they need to continue growing.    "We are proud to welcome the FIA and our fellow Member Clubs from across Asia-Pacific to the Philippines.”   The Congress follows a period of significant activity for the FIA across the region.  The FIA has expanded its  Safe Mobility 4 All & 4 Life  programme into Asia-Pacific, supporting Member Clubs and authorities with training and practical tools to improve road safety, while initiatives including the  FIA Innovation Challenge  continue to showcase Club-led solutions which can be shared and scaled across the Federation.  Across motor sport, the region continues to play an important role at every level of competition, from grassroots participation and regional championships through to the FIA's major World Championships with Malaysia set to host the Bahrain Grand Prix in the days following the congress.  The FIA Member Club structure forms the backbone of the federation’s governance and operations, with each full Member Club holding voting rights across the FIA’s elections and regulatory decisions. Clubs are grouped into two primary categories, with some serving in both roles:   Mobility Clubs – provide mobility services and represent the interest of road users, with a focus on road safety, travel and tourism, consumer rights, and sustainable mobility  National Sporting Authorities (ASNs) – govern and develop motorsport at a national level, are responsible for sporting events, issuing licenses, and engagement across regulations   Within the FIA there are four Mobility Regions and 6 sport zones. The FIA Asia Pacific Congress will welcome Member Clubs from across the region. The global FIA Membership is comprised of 246 clubs across five continents, connecting over 80 million members.      -ENDS-      For media enquiries please contact:   Geri Sherwin, Director of Presidential and Mobility Communications:  gsherwin@fia.com   George Mitchell, Mobility Communications Officer:  gmitchell@fia.com        About the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile    The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. title: Clean Sweeps for Morelli and Perico to Win Blockbuster FIA Karting World Cup
summary: Sport news The 2026 FIA Karting World Cup has concluded with victory for two of the brightest racing stars who delivered world-class performances to win every one of their heats, super heats and finals over the weekend.  Yuri Morelli in the OK-N category becomes the third ever winner of the title adding his name on the cup alongside 2024 winner Kyuho Lee and 2025 winner Manuel Scognamiglio. Morelli converted pole to three heat wins, a super heat win and a final victory to secure the title in spectacular style.  In OK-N Junior, the honours were awarded to Niccolò Perico who also delivered a perfect weekend winning every heat, his super heat and a cruise to victory in the final as the undoubted star of this World Cup. The AMG Petronas Mercedes Formula 1 team junior driver wins his first FIA Karting title and secures his position as one of the most exciting young drivers to watch.  John Han secured the 2026 Academy Junior Title after a tense final race which was ultimately won by Max Sulin of Finland. The Hong Kong driver’s points advantage heading into the final round allowed him to comfortably cruise to the chequered flag in second place and still secure the title with a 51 points gap to runner-up Domenico Coco.  Han’s Academy victory is the second FIA title he has collected in as many months after he won the 2026 FIA Karting Arrive and Drive Junior title in September.   OK-N    Super Heats   Heading into the final day of action at the FIA Karting World Cup, Cristian Blandino and Yuri Morelli were tied on a perfect 150 points with three heat wins each leaving the Super Heats this morning to unbreak the deadlock and determine the polesitter for the final race.  Morelli was first to defend his super heat lead and delivered a statement drive to cross the line over a second ahead of Manuel Scognamiglio who gained two places to stay well in contention this weekend to retain his 2025 title. Morelli’s super heat victory, along with a perfect record in the heats and his fastest time recorded in timed qualifying therefore guaranteed the Brazilian pole position in the final before Blandino contested his super heat.  The contest for the remaining front row position played out between Lamberto Ferrari and Cristian Blandino who held a 14-point advantage in the intermediate classification standings. Ferrari’s first lap overtake into the lead left him just two points behind Blandino in the standings, relying on Blandino to drop a further place if he was to dent Blandino’s perfect run of heat wins this weekend.  Jercan’s gain of five positions and into third provided the most hope for Ferrari but in a final charge to retain his run of victories, Blandino regained control of the heat to take the chequered flag and secure a second position start for the final alongside Morelli setting up a blockbuster finale between the two so far unbeaten drivers in OK-N this weekend.    Final   Off the line Blandino had the better start to claim the lead by the first corner, but into the second lap a three-way scrap for the lead ensued with Morelli, Blandino and Ferrari all aware of the finality of this race to determine the 2026 World Cup winner.  Morelli immediately turned offensive to regain the lead, unwilling to allow a gap to build to the Italian duo of Ferrari and Blandino. 2025 winner Scognamiglio initially fell down the order but soon recovered into fourth to join his compatriots in their quest to keep the World Cup Italian in 2026.  Morelli’s tactics paid off for the Brazilian as he found pace and eased into the race, allowing the Italians behind to choose their challenger to him. Following an exchange of positions, Scognamiglio emerged as the Italian to mount the strongest challenge. However, by this point a two second gap had already built to Morelli, presenting a mountain to climb if anyone is to unseat him from the top step of the podium.  Scognamiglio and Morelli raced through the middle section of the race as the quickest drivers on track, matching each other’s sectors and leaving the field behind to watch if the World Cup would have a new or a returning name etched onto the trophy.  For polesitter and unbeaten heat winner Morelli, the time to Scognamiglio never dropped and as he rounded the final corners, he could taste the World Cup glory ahead of him as he secured his status as the third ever FIA Karting World Cup winner in OK-N. After a faultless and assured performance all weekend, Morelli had earnt his place in the FIA Karting history books and inherited the title Scognamiglio behind him won so memorably in Cremona last year.  For Blandino the final race turned into the first hurdle of the weekend he couldn’t leap over. After losing control of the race at the start he wasn’t able to recover and spent most of his race in a battle for third with Lamberto Ferrari, ultimately won by Ferrari who completed the podium positions.  Reigning Academy Trophy Senior winner Albie Lapper, who scraped into the final, made it up into 28th position with a gain of 11 spots whilst Giuseppe Piccolo’s race ended early for a technical infringement after he had been enjoying a decent run in the final.   Yuri Morelli, CRG Racing Team, said:    “I have no words to describe this feeling, it’s a unique feeling, I think I’ve never felt anything like that before. For me the race was pretty automatic, I was focused on the main objective which was winning the race which was hard but I tried my best and thankfully everything went right”   Top 3 in the FIA Karting World Cup (OK-N)  1. Yuri Morelli (BRA, CRG Racing Team)  2. Manuel Scognamiglio (ITA, Pantano by Dam)  3. Lamberto Ferrari (ITA, ASD Monster K Factory Team)   OK-N Junior    Super Heats   Niccolò Perico, the only junior driver to score a perfect 150 points through the heats, occupied the Super Heat pole position and led throughout the super heat, only facing light pressure from Elton Hedfors who kept within a second throughout the heat. Perico’s super heat win and unrivalled run of form this weekend therefore guaranteed him pole position for the final as the best placed driver in the OK-N Junior category.  In the battle for the remaining front row position, Luigi D’Ascoli faced the threat of a surging John Mclellan who gained seven positions to challenge for the super heat win. D’Ascoli ultimately managed to keep the American driver at bay with a half second gap over the line to confirm an Italian front-row lockout for the final.  Friday’s polesitter, Schelvis Moron, delivered the drive of the morning, making up ground in the Super Heat to finish in third position after starting in tenth place. His disqualification from his first heat set his weekend back but his successful day yesterday with a win and second place resulted in a ninth-place start for the final.   Final   When the Italian front row showdown commenced, both drivers raced fairly and cleanly over the opening laps of the deciding race for the junior World Cup honours. John Mclellan triggered the strongest challenge from behind and began to climb into the top five during the early laps, with the leading positions ahead of him unchanged.  Mclellan was soon joined by Troy Ferguson as they commenced an American push through the field with both drivers making up a series of places to quickly occupy fourth and fifth by the halfway point. Ferguson, in particular, began to deliver what will become a memorable and skilful performance from his 13th place start on the grid.  At the sharp end of the race, Perico, D’Ascoli and Hedfors initially broke away with the American tussle for fourth unfolding allowing Perico to steadily build a buffer from his nearest challenger. This weekend Perico has delivered an exemplary performance which no other driver could come close to, from qualifying in third position to his heat pace and final dominance, he has shown why the young driver is a Mercedes AMG Petronas Formula 1 Team junior driver.  Perico went on to cross the line with over five seconds to his nearest rival, an incredible display of race pace that will catch the eye of the motor sport world. As the Italian national anthem rang out across the circuit, the assembled crowd were sure to have witnessed a rising star of the sport and one of the most exciting prospects in karting.  Behind Perico, attention had turned to the final spot of the podium where Troy Ferguson had sliced the gap to Hedfors and made the crucial move into third position with Mclellan following his coattails. The gap to D’Ascoli was seemingly a challenge too far for Ferguson but in the closing laps he found a burst of pace, similar to the final lap push he unleashed in Malaysia last year to win the Arrive and Drive World Cup, and he successfully gained second position on track.  However, a post-race front fairing penalty meant Ferguson’s second step on the podium was sadly short lived as D’Ascoli regained second and Mclellan was promoted to the final step of the podium.  Elsewhere in the final, Friday polesitter Schelvis Moron made contact with Titz to prematurely end his race whilst Sulpizio and Moehring were the other big beneficiaries of the final race to end within the top ten. The biggest gain of the day however went to Italian driver Raffaele Mini who climbed a total of 15 places.   Niccolò Perico, FIA Karting World Cup Winner (OK-N Junior), said:    “Super happy about it, I don’t even have words about it. It was amazing I just really want to thank everyone that has supported me this weekend. All the team, KR, IAME, my mechanics, my family, Mercedes. We’ll see what we can do at the next one but for now we’ll be about this one.”   Top 3 in the FIA Karting World Cup (OK-N Junior)  1. Niccolò Perico (ITA, KR)  2. Luigi D’Ascoli (ITA, Modena)  3. John Mclellan (USA, Ward)   Academy Junior    Heats   Heading into the final set of heats, Domenico Coco held the advantage in the standings but needed a perfect run on Sunday as well as a mishap from Han to stand a realistic chance of closing the 38-point gap to Han and winning the Academy title on home soil today.  Sensing the pressure that Coco was placing on him this weekend, Han strived to put himself in a strong position for the final, immediately passing Gorlero Pizarro in the final heat to take the win and bring himself into second place in the provisional standings awaiting Coco’s attempt.  Coco initially carried his strong run of form this weekend into the super heats and quickly closed in on Grignet and into the heat lead in the second lap. The Italian driver’s attempt to pull away was hampered by a dual challenge for the lead from Sulin and Shimbashi who were both in contention for top five grid positions for the final.  A last lap sprint to the line ended with Shimbashi taking the chequered flag ahead of Sulin and Coco in third. Coco’s third place finish in the heat left him level on points with both Gorlero Pizarro and Han in the standings leaving qualifying practice to determine the final grids.  Gorlero Pizarro would therefore take pole for the final alongside Han on the front row ahead of Coco and Max Sulin on the second row. Han’s final heat victory was ultimately crucial to hand him the advantage heading into the final race where he can seal the deal and win the 2026 Academy Junior title.   Final   Off the line Han delivered one of the starts of the weekend to sweep past Gorlero Pizarro in the opening corner and into firm control of both the final and the title race. In the opening laps the biggest drama however came from Zoltan Coigny, first round winner and third position in the standings, who dramatically retired on lap four to leave only Coco as Han’s rival to the title this year.  Max Sulin occupied second position, keeping Coco at bay from the lead, but as the gap to Han significantly reduced the Hong Kong driver lost the lead of the race to the Finnish driver leaving him unprotected from Coco behind.  Coco, however, in turn, faced the pace of earlier heat winner Shimbashi who continued to gain places and entered the podium spots by the halfway point of the race at the expense of the home hope.  It was the contest for the top ten places however which attracted the most on track action. Juozaitis unleashed impressive race pace along with Kevin Pentell, but the charge of the day belonged to William Nielsen who banked an impressive 18 overtakes to ultimately finish in ninth place.  As the race neared its conclusion, Han sat comfortably in second place knowing a clean end to the race would be more than enough to secure the 2026 title. Keeping to within a second of Sulin, Han began to sense danger as Shimbashi approached behind, the Hong Kong driver keen to end his incredible weekend on a high, triggering his defensive end to the race.  As the chequered flag fell it was a first Academy Trophy race win for Max Sulin capping off an incredible weekend for the Finnish driver who finished half a second clear of John Han who kept Shimbashi at bay to occupy the second spot of the podium.  Han’s second place finish was, in the end, more than enough to win the 2026 FIA Karting Academy Trophy, ending the season with an impressive 51 points gap to his nearest rival, Coco.   John Han, 2026 FIA Karting Academy Trophy Junior winner, said:    “It’s a very amazing 2026 for me, having three podiums in three races and managing to win the championship!”    Top 3 in the final round of the 2026 FIA Karting Academy Trophy Junior   1. title: F1 - 2026 Singapore Grand Prix Post-Race Press Conference Transcript
summary: Sport news  DRIVERS   1 – Max VERSTAPPEN (Red Bull Racing)   2 – Charles LECLERC (Ferrari)   3 – Kimi ANTONELLI (Mercedes)     TRACK INTERVIEWS    (Conducted by Jenson Button)      Q: Kimi, can we have a word with you first, please? Kimi, it seemed like quite a quiet race for you until it wasn't, and then there was action everywhere. How was the race for you, getting a podium? I think we're all quite surprised, but you pulled it out of the bag, as you always do.   Kimi ANTONELLI:  Yeah, I mean, it was a very tough race out there, but really happy with the podium at the end. I managed to take advantage of the fight of Lando and Lewis and to make the move on both, and to bring home P3 is a great result for the team. And yeah, very happy with that.    Q: I'm sure it's nice to stand on the podium, and I have to let you know this bit of information, but the next race in Austin, you could clinch the World Championship. How does that feel?   KA:  Can I really? Well, let's not worry about that. Let's try to do the best weekend as possible and finish the job.    Q: Charles, it looked like you were going to give Max a run for his money at the start of the race there. Great start, the pace in the first stint looked pretty awesome as well, and then it sort of fell away a little bit.   Charles LECLERC:  Yeah, we were quite strong at the beginning of the race, then we started degrading a little bit more in the first stint. But then we did a slightly different strategy to Max with the Safety Car. I believed in it until the very end, but I pushed a lot at the beginning of that last stint and then degraded a bit more than the others. But yeah, I gave it all and I don't regret anything. I don't think there was much more to do today, apart from maybe being a bit more aggressive at the start. That's the way it is.    Q: You've spoken over the last couple of races that you guys have lost a little bit of pace to the front. Do you still feel like that after this race? Obviously, Max won the race, but you seem a lot closer and you're in front of Mercedes and McLaren.   CL:  Yeah, I still feel that way. However, it's true that we brought some small new parts to the car, which maybe helped us to do another step forward, but it's not enough. We'll push until the end and we've still got to bring some new things to the car to be at the level. But I think today we had a good pace overall.    Q: Nice work. Max, a masterclass. Your first ever… I can't believe I'm saying this, your first ever Singapore Grand Prix victory.   Max VERSTAPPEN:  Yeah, it's taken a while, but I think this race was very good. I mean, yeah, we had pace when we needed to have it on the Soft tyre and on the Medium, even though I think the Medium tyre for everyone was a bit more of a struggle. But it worked out, so of course very happy to win here.    Q: Were you a little nervous before the start? It's not been the easiest for you, the starts over the last couple of...   MV:  Yeah, well, you always try to do your best and luckily it was just good enough.    Q: Yeah, so the last couple of races we've seen you win on a fast-flowing track like Sepang and then a stop-start sort of track here in Singapore. You guys are on the up. It seems to be working for you guys wherever you go.   MV:  I think the last few races have been really positive for us. It's just great to see and yeah, we have a lot of motivation in the team to try and deliver even more results. So yeah, it's a really good group of people. I really enjoy working with them and yeah, hopefully we can have a bit more fun till the end of the year.    PRESS CONFERENCE      Q: Max, you've done it. Very well done. You've won in Singapore. It looked completely dominant. Just how smooth was it for you in the cockpit?   MV:  Well, the start was critical, so that was just good enough. And again, something was not particularly right at the start, so I need to understand what went wrong there. Before releasing the clutch, it didn't feel good. But yeah, it was just good enough. Then we had a few laps with some deployment issues, so that's where Charles almost got me actually into Turn 7. And once we had cleared the deployment problems, yeah, it was fine. The car was really good on the tyres. I could really manage them well. But to be honest, I think it was one of the first times that I've driven in clean air here in Singapore in the race, so I guess that's also nice. And yeah, it's been just a fantastic weekend for us. I mean, we were flying on the Soft, we were okay on the Medium, and then of course with the VSC, I think it was right what Charles did with pitting and going back on a Soft tyre. But yeah, we just had it under control and of course, yeah, really happy to win here.    Q: Just a few more words on the start. You were a bit nervous about it yesterday. Was this a big step forward compared to recent starts?   MV:  Well, like I said, there was something again not right, so I need to understand what went on with the engine before even dropping the clutch, because I think that did hurt my start. So, I just need to understand what went wrong there because it was again not fantastic, you can say that.    Q: What about the radio? I mean, that perhaps was your biggest issue of the whole race. Did you and GP have to speak in code? How did it work?   MV:  Yeah, maybe he was happy that it was not working! I couldn't really say anything. Yeah, he did try at one point to ask me a few things in code, and I think he understood well what I meant or did not do, right. But it's never nice. I've been having difficulty with my radio already the whole season, and this weekend has been particularly bad.    Q: Yeah, so it's been the perfect weekend here in Singapore. It's actually been a very good triple-header for you in Asia, hasn't it? Just how much more can you achieve in the remaining races this year?   MV:  Yeah, I mean, very different tracks that we have gone well at now. That's of course always nice to see. I really think, of course, that our car has taken a really nice step forward. But at the end of the day, yeah, it's just been more driveable and more predictable. That's what I wanted and needed from the car to find that last step to fight up front. And I hope that we can carry that momentum forward. We don't really have anything to win in the championship, right? I think Kimi is miles ahead. For me personally, I don't care if I'm second, third or fourth. Like, yeah, it doesn't do anything. But I just want to have fun till the end, you know, try to go for a day’s success.    Q: Yeah, Max, very well done. Thank you for that. Charles, let's come to you now. Great to see you back on the podium. Just how satisfying was this race for you?   CL:  Well, I mean, happy but not super happy. I mean, second place is a good result, I think, considering the tendency that we've had lately where we were lacking just a little bit of pace. I feel like, at least particularly in qualifying yesterday, we had strong pace. Today in the race, Max had a bit more pace than we did, which was expected, but we were maybe a little bit closer than what we expected as well. So, it was a cool race. I believed in it until the very end, but unfortunately it wasn't quite enough.    Q: Your best chance to pass Max came at the start. Just talk us through those opening 200 metres. Did you think you had him at one point or not?   CL:  I mean, you don't have much time to think in those moments. I just saw that Max had a bit of a difficult start. I had quite a good start, so I went alongside him. Then there wasn't much space anymore, but I would have done exactly the same. And yeah, then it's quite tricky. I mean, I was on the left, a little bit behind him, couldn't see the panels on the right, so you lose a little bit all your references because that's normally on the right that you have your references to brake. I tried to judge it in the best possible way, but Max managed to keep that first place. And then there were a few opportunities in the first three laps when Max had the deployment issue, but I always thought that it was a one-off, so I wasn't really using my battery, which maybe was a mistake. And when I was realising that he had no power at the end of the straight, I couldn't do anything. It was too late for me to use my power. But I don't know if it would have changed much. Maybe, of course, for the first stint it would have helped, but I think eventually they just had too much pace for us.    Q: Do you think anything would have been different if you'd been on a different tyre to Max at the start?   CL:  No, I don't think it would have helped. If anything, it probably would have been worse because the Medium just didn't feel like a great tyre. So, I probably would have lost any flexibility to put Max under a bit more pressure around the pit stop time, even though he was still far. I think with the Medium he would have been further away.    Q: Charles, let's throw it forward. This is your first podium since before the summer break. Is the car now back in a window where you think you can challenge for the podium at every race?   CL:  It's too early to say, but it's true that we've brought some small parts here and there on the car, which maybe helped us to do a step forward. But yes, we cannot forget as well the tendency of the last three races before this one. And the tendency I'm speaking about is that we are losing a little bit of pace compared to Red Bull, compared to Mercedes and also compared to McLaren. But McLaren have been struggling a little bit more maybe in Sepang and here. But yeah, at the end of the day, it's all about who brings the upgrades as early as possible. And hopefully we'll be the ones to do a bigger step than the others at the next upgrades we bring.    Q: Charles, thank you for that. Well done to you. And Kimi, great race by you as well. You took your chances today. Just how much did you enjoy it out there?   KA:  Yeah, I mean, the heat was not very enjoyable. Running behind other cars was quite hot. But I think it was a good way to end the weekend, a very good way to end the weekend. I feel like it was a very progressive weekend, where we started off the pace and I've definitely been struggling with the new package. But the team did incredibly well on putting the car in a better window. And now we understand a lot more the aero package, how it works, which is very different compared to the old one. And it's about trying to find the right window for the car. But all in all, I feel like we're seeing the light at the end of the tunnel and we're going to keep pushing on this package because also on my side, I want to help the team as much as possible in trying to understand it, also to understand which way to take for the future car as well.    Q: Well, on the topic of the new package, are you now convinced it's faster than the old one?   KA:  I think on this track, not yet. On this track, where you have a lot of slow speed, still not quite there in terms of performance. It's just because with the old package, you know exactly where to put the car, which window, and the car works very nicely. With this new package, we see the potential, the performance that it can bring, and I do feel it in certain corners. But the window is just too small of where the car operates at this moment. So also in driving, it's very sensitive to any differences that you do in the way you approach a corner or how you attack braking. So, I feel like, yes, the package is going to be faster and it's going to be, yeah, I think it can be a good step forward once we understand how to use the full potential.    Q: Okay, were there any dramas for you in this race? I mean, at one point you came on the radio and said, "I have no brakes." That sounded serious. What happened? How did you resolve that?   KA:  Well, just trying to lift and coast before every braking and to arrive a bit slower and put less pressure on the pedal. Because especially on the restart of the VSC, when I went to brake, nothing happened. I had really poor stopping, brake power and I almost went into the wall. So, it was just very tricky out there, and also the pedal was very long. But it was also kind of expected. You know, I've run three-quarters of the race behind a car in dirty air and obviously being so hot. Plus, we also had the sensor issue on the brakes, so we didn't even have the data about the brakes. We didn't know exactly what temperature they were running, so it was all about feeling. But they were hot because I could even smell it, so it was not very pleasant.    Q: Kimi, final one from me. The world title is now within touching distance. You can clinch it next time out in Austin. How much are you going to think about that? Will you dare to dream about it on the long flight home?   KA:  For sure, but at the same time, I know it's very close, I know it's there, but I just need to make sure that I keep doing the best I can. You know, the mindset is always the same, to go out there and win and perform the best way I can. I think this weekend I haven't particularly driven that well. I felt like I could have done a better job, but I feel confident that, you know, a week to reset and I'm really looking forward to being back in Austin. But at the end of the day, if I don't do my job well, then the result won't come. So in order to achieve what I want, I need to perform, as simple as that.    QUESTIONS FROM THE FLOOR     Q: (Ronald Vording – Motorsport.com) It's a question to Max. It's now two years in a row that Red Bull turned around quite a difficult start of the season. But how different have those two turnarounds been? Because last year it looked a lot about set-up and finding the potential, and this looks more related to just, physically, parts on the car.   MV:  Yes, exactly. And you answered it already yourself. Yeah, two completely different cars as well, right, with the regulations. Also, two completely different problems that we had to find lap time. Plus, of course, also this year with the engine side of things, I think for everyone it's been sometimes a bit complicated to get the most out of it. But from race one to now, I think we've gained a lot of experience. Of course, still not where we want to be, but I guess everyone will say the same thing. But we have learned so much and definitely also on the car side have fixed a lot of our weaknesses. And yeah, we just need to keep improving, keep learning this year that we can apply also into next year.    Q: (Michael Butterworth – Xinhua News Agency) Max, you said you wanted to have some fun between now and the end of the season. Do you think your car is now in the place where you can fight for victory on every track that we have coming up from now to the end of the year?   MV:  I mean, it's very difficult to say and I don't want to say now that I will be in the fight in Austin. But yeah, the last few weekends have been great. But I just take it race by race and once we are in Austin, then we'll see how it will go there. But it's again a very different track. From what I saw in WEC, the track is incredibly bumpy. Oh my God, yeah, I’ll probably need to order a new spine, I think, after the weekend. Yeah, I'll become like RoboCop. Yeah, crazy. That's again a new challenge for everyone, to deal with those bumps. And then we just go from there. We have to go to Mexico, again high altitude, everything will run super hot, and we need to see how the engine is going to perform in that altitude, how the car is behaving, because it's very different. So there are so many different things that you can get right or wrong in those races, but we'll see.    Q: (Luke Smith – The Athletic) Max, you talked through Turn 1 and saying that you managed to just about hold on. Could you actually precisely break down what you did at that corner to just keep it around the outside? And was there ever a moment you thought, "Ah, this position's gone," and just leave it be?   MV:  No, I was only here to win, so I had to do everything I could to try and make sure that it was very difficult for Charles to go deep into the corner. So I guess that was the only way to try and stop him from getting the lead. Luckily, I mean, he's a very experienced driver and we kept it clean. It was actually really nice, I think. But yeah, it's always very hard to judge what is the right braking point, but I think it just worked out.    Q: (Minh Son Khuat – Viettel) Hello, Max. First of all, congratulations on winning both the Sprint   and the Grand Prix this weekend. So when you crossed the finish line today, what was the very first thought that went through your mind? Because this is the track that you haven't conquered for a long time.   MV:  Yeah, it was a bit of a relief, of course, to win here. I think when you win for the first time on a track, it's always very special and nice. So yeah, I was very happy just with the whole weekend. And at the same time, I was probably also very happy that it was over. The race was long enough and I was sweating a lot.    Q: (Laurine Slingerland – Nu.nl) A question for Max. Congrats on the win, first. How was it for you to have GP on the podium, especially after a day that he maybe had to talk more than ever because of the issues?   MV:  Yeah, didn't expect that. Yeah, I remember he said to me last year in Vegas, "This might be the last time I'm on the podium." I said, "Don't be silly, we're going to win much more." But I almost jinxed myself there, I guess. And yeah, it was just super nice that they sent him up. Of course, we all know that he is leaving, but I think it was very special to share the podium here on a track that we had not won together. So very nice to see him up there.    Q: (Luu Trung Kien Tran – Viettel) I have a question for Charles. At the time you were chasing your   team-mate Lewis Hamilton, were you confident that you could overtake Lewis, knowing the team may not issue team orders?   CL:  Well, I mean, we were on very different strategies and I arrived with a much fresher tyre. So I mean, yeah, I think at that point it made very much sense to not lose time between us because I was still in the chase of Max and trying to win the race. Even though it was a long shot, we had to put all our chances on our side. So I wasn't particularly overthinking it. I had a very strong tyre advantage and Lewis didn't make my life difficult because it was very clear that as a team, we couldn't lose too much time.    Q: (Karen Vera – Tatler Asia) Hello, Max. You mentioned earlier about just having fun throughout   the rest of the season. When did this realisation come to you? Was it very recent or did you have this always in mind?   MV:  I mean, I think the car definitely felt a lot nicer from Baku onwards. It's just been a lot more balanced. And then naturally, of course, when you can compete a bit further up front without having too many issues with the car compared to the beginning of the year, where it was actually sometimes a bit scary to drive, yeah, that makes it a lot nicer. And yeah, the way that we turned that around and actually the big progress that we have made this year, yeah, that makes it of course a lot nicer. And when you can add a few wins as well, it's just nice. And we're not in a championship fight, and that's why I think till the end, yeah, we just try to have a good time and try to add more podiums and hopefully a few wins.    Q: (Ronald Vording – Motorsport.com) It's a question to Kimi for a change. George said in the media pen that he thinks after the Baku upgrade, Red Bull is now the team to beat in Formula One. Do you agree with that or do you think that it's also partly related to your upgrade package and still not unlocking the full potential of it?   KA:  I think, yes, probably mostly us not extracting the maximum out of the new package. I mean, of course Red Bull has done an incredible step forward, but as well, Max has probably been more comfortable with the car and just extracting more out of it. So, it's a combination of things. But for sure they've done a good step forward. And on our side, it's just, as I said, we're just trying to understand how to extract more potential out of it because we do see the gains, we do see what it could bring. It's just that the window is very small at the moment where the car operates and is very sensitive to the way you drive it, the way you take a corner, the way you brake. So it reacts very differently. So hopefully now in Austin, we have three free practices, so we can be very open-minded with set-up and hopefully we can find a way and we can use the full potential of the package and finally see the gains. But I think the team did an incredible job this weekend on just putting the car in a better place and allowing me to get the confidence. And now it's a starting point to keep working and keep extracting the potential.    ENDS     FIA Formula One World Championship    Formula 1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026Formula 100 Sunday, October 11, 2026 - 5:53pm  Sunday, October 11, 2026 - 5:53pm

title: F1 – Verstappen takes commanding Singapore victory ahead of Leclerc and Antonelli
summary: Sport news Max Verstappen took his first Singapore Grand Prix victory with a controlled drive at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, beating Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc by 7.335 seconds as championship leader Kimi Antonelli claimed third following a late battle for the final podium place.  The Red Bull driver led throughout the 62-lap race to secure his 73rd career victory, managing a one-stop strategy through two Virtual Safety Car periods. Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri finished fourth and fifth for McLaren, ahead of Lewis Hamilton, whose attempt to complete the race without a second stop left him vulnerable in the closing stages.  At the start, Leclerc made a strong getaway from second, but Verstappen moved across to protect the inside and retained the lead into Turn 1. Hamilton held third ahead of Antonelli, while Norris and Piastri avoided further contact after their collision in the Sprint.  Further back, Liam Lawson moved into seventh and Nico Hülkenberg and Carlos Sainz gained places to run eighth and 10th respectively. Oliver Bearman emerged ahead of Haas team-mate Esteban Ocon after an early scrap, while George Russell began his recovery from the back of the grid, reaching 15th by lap five.  Leclerc initially stayed within range of Verstappen, running six tenths behind and able to use Overtake Mode. The leader gradually eased away, however, as the opening stint developed.  The first interruption came when Gabriel Bortoleto stopped near the pit lane exit with an apparent gearbox problem. A Virtual Safety Car allowed his Audi to be recovered, before a subsequent fire required marshals to extinguish the flames and prompted a brief closure of the pit lane entry.  Once racing resumed, Verstappen continued to set the pace. By lap 15 his advantage had grown to 2.6 seconds, while Hamilton, starting on medium tyres, was coming under pressure from Antonelli and the McLarens.  Ferrari brought Hamilton in on lap 19 for soft tyres, sending him back out seventh behind Lawson. He passed the Racing Bulls driver on lap 21, but the early stop left Ferrari considering whether another visit would be required before the finish.  Antonelli stopped for mediums on lap 24, with Leclerc following one lap later. The Monegasque rejoined narrowly ahead of Hamilton, who reported losing time behind his team-mate despite running the softer compound.  Verstappen extended his opening stint, holding a 17.9-second advantage over Norris by lap 28 as Piastri ran third. Behind them, Russell continued to progress, passing Ocon at Turn 16 and gaining further positions as others stopped.  Alpine lost Franco Colapinto to a suspected gearbox problem, while Hülkenberg’s pit stop helped Russell climb to ninth. Antonelli, meanwhile, reported fluid leaking around his feet, adding another concern to a race in which he had already received warnings for exceeding track limits.  Verstappen finally stopped on lap 33, switching to medium tyres and retaining the lead. Norris followed and emerged behind Antonelli, before a slower stop for Piastri left the Australian six seconds behind his team-mate in sixth.  With the leading stops completed, attention shifted to tyre endurance and the contrasting strategies at Ferrari. Hamilton remained behind Leclerc, while Antonelli received a black and white flag for track limits and asked Mercedes to investigate unusual behaviour from his car.  A second Virtual Safety Car followed when Lance Stroll stopped at Turn 15 with a clutch issue. Leclerc and Antonelli used the interruption to make their second stops, while Russell came in for his first as the neutralisation ended, reducing the benefit available to the Mercedes driver.  Hamilton consequently moved into second, with Leclerc returning third around 10 seconds behind him. Antonelli rejoined between the McLarens in fifth, although he subsequently reported braking difficulties. Mercedes attributed the fluid around his feet to heat soak.  Piastri then made an additional stop on lap 42 after suffering a slow puncture, returning in sixth. At Ferrari, Hamilton’s remaining tyre life became increasingly significant as Leclerc closed on fresher rubber.  On lap 46, Leclerc passed his team-mate for second, but Verstappen remained 15 seconds ahead. Russell gained ninth from Pierre Gasly at Turn 7 two laps later, before his progress was checked by Hülkenberg.  The contest for third intensified as Hamilton’s pace faded. Norris closed to within half a second, but when Hamilton ran wide defending, Antonelli seized the opportunity to pass the McLaren. The Italian then overtook Hamilton at Turn 16 to take third.  Norris soon followed past the Ferrari to claim fourth. Piastri also caught Hamilton and, after several attempts, completed his move at Turn 16 for fifth, leaving the seven-time champion sixth.  Hamilton was investigated for leaving the track and gaining an advantage during the battle, but no further action was required. After the finish, he apologised to Ferrari over the radio for the strategy outcome. Norris received a warning about a potential sensor issue, while Verstappen encountered radio difficulties as Red Bull considered its options for another interruption.  Leclerc reduced the deficit over the final laps, but Verstappen remained comfortably clear to win in 1:42:00.785. Antonelli finished 24.573 seconds behind the winner, with Norris and Piastri a further 15.933 and 25.071 seconds back respectively.  Lawson secured seventh ahead of Hülkenberg and Russell, while Isack Hadjar completed the points in 10th. Gasly finished 11th, followed by Bearman, Ocon, Sainz, Arvid Lindblad and Fernando Alonso. Sergio Pérez was 17th, with Alexander Albon classified 18th despite retiring and Valtteri Bottas 19th. title: FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem meets with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev as Baku Celebrates a Decade of Racing
summary: FIA news His Excellency Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), met with His Excellency Ilham Aliyev, President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, in Baku today to discuss shared priorities across motorsport and mobility.  The meeting, which took place during the Baku Grand Prix as the city celebrated a decade of racing on its iconic streets, provided an opportunity to discuss Azerbaijan’s continued development as a major international sporting destination, its established position within global motorsport, and opportunities to strengthen cooperation between the country and the FIA.  Azerbaijan has become an important destination on the international sporting calendar, with Baku providing one of Formula 1’s most distinctive city-centre settings and attracting fans and visitors from around the world.  The Presidents also discussed the wider role of mobility in supporting economic growth and connectivity, as well as the importance of road safety and sustainable transport as Azerbaijan continues to invest in its infrastructure and international connectivity.   FIA President, H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem said:   “It was a pleasure to meet with His Excellency President Ilham Aliyev and discuss our shared ambitions for the continued development of motorsport and mobility in Azerbaijan.    “The success of Formula 1 in Baku demonstrates what can be achieved through long-term commitment, strong organisation and a clear vision for the role that major sporting events can play in bringing people together and showcasing a country to the world. My congratulations on a fantastic ten years of racing and I look forward to many more.    “Our discussions also extended beyond motorsport. As the global federation for mobility organisations, the FIA is committed to working with governments and our Member Clubs such as the Azerbaijan Automobile Federation to make mobility safer, more accessible and more sustainable. I look forward to continuing our collaboration with our partners in Azerbaijan across these important areas.”   President Ben Sulayem’s visit comes as the FIA continues to strengthen its engagement across the region through its global network of Member Clubs and partners, including the Azerbaijan Automobile Federation and its President Anar Alakbarov.  The FIA has placed significant emphasis on growing motorsport participation and strengthening the pathway from grassroots competition to the highest levels of the sport, while using its global mobility network to advance road safety, sustainable mobility and accessibility. Azerbaijan’s position at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, alongside continued investment in transport and infrastructure, provides opportunities for further collaboration across both pillars of the FIA’s work.  The meeting formed part of President Ben Sulayem’s programme in Azerbaijan, bringing together government, motorsport and mobility stakeholders to discuss opportunities to further develop the FIA’s activities in the country and wider region.        ENDS    About the FIA   The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.  Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 246 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. It develops and enforces regulations for motor sport, including seven FIA World Championships, to ensure worldwide competitions are safe and fair for all. title: WEC: Alpine on pole at Fuji after rain leads to qualifying cancellation
summary: Sport news Heavy rain swept across Fuji Speedway ahead of the scheduled start of the LMGT3 qualifying session, which began on time but was red-flagged after François Heriau went off in his #21 VISTA AF Corse Ferrari.  The decision was then taken to cancel the remaining qualifying sessions due to the forecast of heavier rain and fog at Fuji Speedway.  That meant that, in accordance with the regulations, the grid was set according to the best times from the three Free Practice sessions held across Friday and Saturday morning.  Victor Martins’ FP2 time of 1m40.594s ensured that the #36 Alpine will start from pole position, marking the first-ever WEC pole for the A424 Hypercar.  It was a double celebration for the French manufacturer as the #35 car will join its sister Hypercar on the front row, putting Alpine in a strong position to defend last year’s victory at the venue.  Second on the grid should initially have been the #007 Aston Martin Valkyrie, but it was demoted to fourth after receiving a penalty for causing a collision in the morning’s FP3 session.  Starting third on the grid will be the #17 Genesis Magma Hypercar, meaning the Korean manufacturer will begin tomorrow’s race from by far its best-ever starting position.  In the LMGT3 category, the #77 Proton Competition Ford Mustang will start from pole position after setting the fastest FP2 time on Friday afternoon.
