title: F1 – Verstappen beats Ferrari pair to take Singapore Grand Prix pole
summary: Sport news Max Verstappen took his first Singapore Grand Prix pole position with a lap of 1:31.373, beating Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc by 0.054s as Lewis Hamilton finished third after setting the pace in the opening two segments of Qualifying.  Verstappen’s first Q3 attempt proved decisive at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, where several leading drivers failed to improve on their final runs. Leclerc found time to move ahead of Hamilton, but fell narrowly short of denying the Red Bull driver a second pole of the weekend following his top spot in Sprint Qualifying.  Conditions remained humid throughout the session. The opening segment began with several drivers encountering difficulties. Haas’ Esteban Ocon locked up at Turn 13 and reported a braking problem before reversing back onto the circuit, while Aston Martin’s Lance Stroll also ran into trouble at Turn 7.  Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar, who had retired from the Sprint earlier in the day, suffered further mechanical problems. After running deep and reporting that his engine had switched off, the Frenchman restarted and returned to the pits. However, another issue prevented him from recording a representative lap.  Norris initially headed the timesheet with a lap of 1:33.047, just 0.029s ahead of Piastri. Verstappen and Hamilton followed as the leading teams began to establish their pace. Russell reported a smell of burning and asked Mercedes to monitor his brakes. Hülkenberg and Bearman, meanwhile, showed competitive pace after scoring points in the Sprint.  Hamilton subsequently moved to the front and lowered his benchmark to 1:32.429. Leclerc joined him at the top to give Ferrari the first two positions, while Antonelli had a lap deleted for exceeding track limits.  Further down the order, late improvements changed the battle for progression. Lindblad and Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto moved clear of danger, while both Aston Martin drivers were eliminated. Fernando Alonso finished 17th, ahead of Williams’ Alex Albon and Stroll. Cadillac’s Sergio Pérez and Valtteri Bottas were 20th and 21st respectively, with Hadjar last without a time.  Antonelli set the early Q2 benchmark at 1:32.165, but Hamilton quickly displaced him with a lap of 1:31.766, almost four tenths faster. Verstappen was initially more than half a second behind the Ferrari driver and reported problems with his gear shifts.  Hamilton improved again on his second run, posting 1:31.529 to remain fastest. Verstappen closed the gap with a lap of 1:31.639, while Norris and Leclerc also progressed comfortably to the final segment.  The contest for the remaining Q3 places was closer. Lawson, Lindblad and Audi’s Nico Hülkenberg occupied the final three places in the top 10 after the initial runs, leaving Gasly outside the cut. The Frenchman was two tenths behind Hülkenberg before finding six tenths on his final run.  The Alpine driver improved substantially on his final attempt to secure progression alongside both Racing Bulls drivers. Hülkenberg also found time, but his improvement was insufficient and he was eliminated in 11th.  Haas drivers Oliver Bearman and Ocon finished 12th and 13th, ahead of Williams’ Carlos Sainz and Bortoleto. Franco Colapinto was 16th in the second Alpine after clipping the barrier at Turn 17 on his final lap.  Verstappen then seized the initiative in Q3, setting the eventual pole time on his opening attempt. Hamilton produced a strong middle sector but crossed the line in 1:31.496, leaving him 0.123s behind, while Antonelli recorded 1:31.562.  The final runs brought little change among the front runners. Neither Verstappen nor Hamilton improved, but Leclerc lowered his time to 1:31.427 to secure a place on the front row.  Antonelli remained fourth, 0.189s from pole, with Norris fifth on 1:31.712 and Russell sixth on 1:31.747. Russell faces a grid penalty following an engine change. Piastri improved by more than three tenths on his final attempt, but his 1:31.860 left him seventh. Piastri’s result followed his recovery from the Sprint, in which he and team mate Norris had been involved in a collision.  Gasly also gained ground late in the session, moving ahead of Lawson to finish eighth with 1:32.225. Lawson’s best lap was 1:32.369, while Lindblad completed the shootout with 1:32.781. At the front, Verstappen’s opening effort had withstood Ferrari’s challenge, securing his first Grand Prix pole at Marina Bay after Hamilton had led both Q1 and Q2.   2026 FIA Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix – Qualifying   1 Max Verstappen Red Bull/Red Bull Ford 1'31.373 - - 2 Charles Leclerc Ferrari 1'31.427 0.054  3 Lewis Hamilton Ferrari 1'31.496 0.123  4 Kimi Antonelli Mercedes 1'31.562 0.189  5 Lando Norris McLaren/Mercedes 1'31.712 0.339  6 George Russell Mercedes 1'31.747 0.374  7 Oscar Piastri McLaren/Mercedes 1'31.860 0.487  8 Pierre Gasly Alpine/Mercedes 1'32.225 0.852  9 Liam Lawson Racing Bulls/Red Bull Ford 1'32.369 0.996  10 Arvid Lindblad Racing Bulls/Red Bull Ford 1'32.781 1.408  11 Nico Hülkenberg Audi 1'32.784 1.411  12 Oliver Bearman Haas/Ferrari 1'32.908 1.535  13 Esteban Ocon Haas/Ferrari 1'33.323 1.950  14 Carlos Sainz Williams/Mercedes 1'33.526 2.153  15 Gabriel Bortoleto Audi 1'33.658 2.285  16 Franco Colapinto Alpine/Mercedes 1'33.787 2.414  17 Fernando Alonso Aston Martin/Honda 1'34.223 2.850  18 Alexander Albon Williams/Mercedes 1'34.289 2.916  19 Lance Stroll Aston Martin/Honda 1'34.946 3.573  20 Sergio Pérez Cadillac/Ferrari 1'35.123 3.750  21 Valtteri Bottas Cadillac/Ferrari 1'35.984 4.611  22 Isack Hadjar Red Bull/Red Bull Ford - - -       FIA Formula One World Championship    F1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026F101 Saturday, October 10, 2026 - 6:26pm  Saturday, October 10, 2026 - 6:26pm

title: F1 - 2026 Singapore Grand Prix Post-Qualifying Press Conference Transcript
summary: Sport news  DRIVERS   1 – Max VERSTAPPEN (Red Bull Racing)    2 – Charles LECLERC (Ferrari)    3 – Lewis HAMILTON (Ferrari)     PARC FERMÉ INTERVIEWS   (Conducted by Jolyon Palmer)     Q: So, down here with your top three, and very much the man to beat at the moment, Max Verstappen. What a job, what a weekend so far. How was the session for you?   Max VERSTAPPEN:  It was good. Just very close. The margins are very close, I think, between us throughout the whole of qualifying. So, of course, very happy to be on pole because this is, of course, the one that I wanted. So, yeah, very happy. I mean, the car has been pretty strong all weekend. Of course, there are always things that you look into that can be better, but it was enough for pole, so very happy with that.    Q: Are you surprised? This is the one, apart from Madrid, that you've not got a win on. For some reason, we've always come here and it's not been a Red Bull circuit, or you've not found yourself in the right window. But this weekend you've had a great drive to win the Sprint, soon to be ahead of your rivals.   MV:  Yeah, new regulations, and I think our car now works a little bit differently compared to the previous regulations, where we're stronger in different areas of a corner. But yeah, we take it. I mean, we have been really on a positive trend, you know, so it's, for us, I think, very special to take a pole here.    Q: All right, well done, Max. We'll come back to you in just a second, if I can break you guys up just for a moment. Charles, great job. You're back on the front row here in Singapore. I have to say, it didn't look like the easiest of sessions for you for a lot of it, but that last lap was fantastic.   Charles LECLERC:  Yeah, let's say that the good lap was on the right lap at the end. But I had a lot of struggles during this qualifying. Q1 and Q2 were very difficult. I had some weird things going on with the brakes, car pulling a bit under braking, which is not so nice on a track like here. But then in Q3, the lap was OK. I did some mistakes. I think there was potential to be on pole today, but Max just did a better job.    Q: We saw a lot of other drivers struggling with the brakes early on. How many changes did you make? We know you guys were running different setups in yesterday's running. Did you converge? It's obviously difficult to know after an intermediate race where to go, I assume.   CL:  Well, I guess, yeah, on my side, I changed a little bit the car to make sure, for the last fine-tunings. I was relatively happy with the car yesterday, so changed a few things, not so much. But yeah, at the end of the day, just a bit of misjudgement in Q3 with the wing. Maybe we could have done a bit of a better job, but I think if you ask all drivers on the grid, everybody can find something on that last lap in Q3.    Q: All right, well done. Front-row start for you. And Lewis, what a job. I've loved watching you drive around this circuit this weekend because it has been animated for you. So much oversteer, you're hanging on to it, but in the end, looks like maybe that cost you in the final sector a couple of times. How do you see that session?   Lewis HAMILTON:  Yeah, another difficult Q3. Congrats to Max, he did a great job. Yeah, we made some changes going into qualifying. The car was feeling so much better, and I really felt like she had more in her. So we were just pushing her more and more through the laps and through the sessions. Q1 and Q2 were awesome. We got to Q3 and snaps in Turn 1 and 3 put me two tenths down. The rest of the lap was good, and then the last lap, just again struggled with snapping. So I think there's a real fine line with our car where it's over the edge or under the limit, and finding that sweet spot is very, very difficult. I think I probably had it in the first two, but you have to look for the progress of the track, the grip coming up, and so you have to kind of react to that. In hindsight, maybe I shouldn't have. So it wasn't great enough for myself.    Q: It's obviously a difficult circuit to overtake, but there's two Ferraris, one Red Bull, Isack Hadjar's right at the back of the grid. Is that some hope for tomorrow? In a strategic race, maybe you can still jump on the top step by the end?   LH:  Yeah, well, I think, I mean, Red Bull have done a fantastic job. You know, they've done a great job with their engine, but I think also with their car. It's obviously a great team, and I think they brought an upgrade in Baku which has really put them at the front. And I think it's really still a good result for us to have two Ferraris up there. We could definitely hopefully work as a team tomorrow to try and hold on to Max and put him under pressure. I think that's the only way it's going to be. I'm sure he's going to be fast, but hopefully together as a team we can potentially, who knows? We'll see if we get ahead of him.    Q: All right, well done, Lewis, and good luck tomorrow, guys. So Max, a couple of races in a row now you've won, but you've had pretty bad starts. I think "terrible" was your own words for the one earlier on today. Are you feeling confident tomorrow, if it's dry, your problems are solved, you can just keep the lead and disappear off in the distance? Or are you still doubting how the Red Bull gets off the line?   MV:  Well, you have to look at it positively. It cannot get worse, so it can only get better, right? So, we'll see how it goes tomorrow.    PRESS CONFERENCE      Q: Very well done, Max, and sensational pole lap by you. It looked like this one meant a lot.   MV:  I mean, it was nice, yeah. It's always good, I think, to be on pole position. I think the whole weekend already we've had a strong car, so I knew it was going to be a tight battle, and I think you could see that throughout qualifying. But yeah, of course, nice to be first.    Q: Fifty is a milestone. Does that mean anything to you in particular?   MV:  Better than 49, not as good as 51. So we just try and keep going.    Q: Tell us more about the session. How did you improve the car? We heard you say at one point that you weren't happy with the shifts.   MV:  Yeah, that stayed, so we just had to live with that. But I think the car has been in the right window the whole weekend, so it was more just fine-tuning and tweaking tiny little bits, and that's what we did.    Q: And after the rain earlier in the day, how were the track conditions?   MV:  Track seemed a little bit slower. If I'm not mistaken, I think we went faster yesterday. So yeah, it's been just a bit slower, less grip maybe from driving in the wet, and yeah, the rubber probably disappeared a little bit.    Q: What about the race? Tell us about the long-run pace of the car in practice, and what do you see as the biggest challenge in the Grand Prix here?   MV:  I think no one really knows about the long runs because we didn't really get to do any. But for me, the most important part is more the start. We know that that's not really been our strong area, so we need to work on that for tomorrow.    Q: What kind of things can you do overnight just to try and improve that?   MV:  Just trying to understand why it keeps going wrong, first of all, and then try to just do a better job tomorrow.    Q: Very well done, Max. Thank you for that. Charles, let's come to you now. You found more than two tenths between the first run and second run of Q3. Just tell us where you found the time and how the car was.   CL:  Well, just in commitment. I just committed a little bit more in Q3, last lap. I had a very difficult qualifying session. I had quite a bit of… I mean, on the brakes, the car was pulling a little bit in Q1, Q2. In Q3, maybe slightly better, but I had this issue on braking that was taking off quite a lot of confidence. And in Q3, I just went for it, no matter how it felt, and yeah, it paid off. But yeah, just struggled to put everything together. I think the car had potential for pole today, but we didn't have a smooth session enough in order to do the job, and Max just did a better job.    Q: But still so close to pole. Can you visualise a part of the lap where it may have slipped away from you?   CL:  Yeah, I mean, Turn 13, Turn 16/17, these probably are the two main ones. But yeah, I'm pretty sure that every driver has got something to gain, one corner or the other. So yeah, it just wasn't enough.    Q: Tell us about tomorrow then. How confident are you in the long-run pace of the car?   CL:  Long-run pace should be fine. I mean, I think in FP1 we didn't do many laps consecutive, but the few we did, the feeling was great. So yeah, confident that we shall be on the pace. The start will be very important. This morning we didn't have a great start, so we'll have to make the perfect start tomorrow.    Q: All right, well done. Thank you very much. And Lewis, if we could come to you now. Still incredibly close to pole. It was so tight between the three of you. Now, you struggled with snapping, your words just a moment ago. Tell us a little bit more about that. What was triggering it?   LH:  I think it's just balance. The car felt good. I think my team, the engineers, did a fantastic job, as well as the mechanics, between the sessions. I think the car felt amazing in Q1 and Q2, and when I finished the laps, I was like, "She's got more in her." And the only way in order to try and extract that is to try and add wing. And in doing so, I think it just tipped it over the edge. It was only like one hole or something like that, but it was just on the knife point, and after that then the car was just snappy, and none of the laps in Q3 are any good. So, I'm grateful to be third, to be honest, given that those laps weren't very good.    Q: Throw it forward to tomorrow, Lewis. We saw a sensational start by you in the wet earlier on today. How confident are you of being able to repeat that in the dry?   LH:  I mean, the right side is hopefully a little bit better to start on. It's obviously a short start, so the start that I had was obviously in the wet, so it's much different when it's dry. And I think tomorrow is dry. It'd be very hard for us to beat Max tomorrow, but there's two Ferraris there, and I think we can hopefully, you know, there might be opportunities for us to work together to try and apply the pressure. They're very, very quick, but I think we have the car in a good place that hopefully we can at least hold on.    QUESTIONS FROM THE FLOOR     Q: (Rodrigo França – Car Magazine Brazil) A question to Charles and Max. Another front row for you in Formula 1, but I would like to ask you to share some memories of the front rows you shared in go-karting. Of course, we all remember the incident in France 14 years ago, so if you can share some memories from that time.   CL:  Which incident are you referring to? There's been quite a few. Yeah, there was the incident that was in... Which track already?   MV:  Val d'Argenton. CL: The double right? Val d'Argenton. Yeah, exactly. Yeah, no, I mean, I was just saying to Max in the cooldown room that the karting days felt like yesterday. I don't have as good of a memory to tell you about the front rows we've had in karting, but there were quite a few. And yeah, it's just nice that we've been following each other and that now we are fighting in Formula 1. He’s a bit too many championships ahead, but hopefully I'll catch one day. It's good to be starting on the front row together, and hopefully I'll get a good start to get ahead.  MV:  Yeah, I think back in the day there were a few drivers that looked like they would make it to Formula 1 or at least had a big chance. Charles was definitely one of them. Yeah, it's good. I mean, it's nice to see, of course, these drivers that you have raced against your whole life, that you race against them also in Formula 1. It means that it was a competitive field when you were doing well. So yeah, it's nice. We've shared a few front rows, so it's good to see.    Q: (Christian Menath – Motorsport-Magazin.com) Another question for Max. Max, you already touched on it this morning after the start in the Sprint, and now again. You said the Racing Bulls, they have, as I mentioned, but they have better starts than you have. Do you know what's the problem? Is it the hardware that you have available in the Red Bull car? How much can the driver influence the start, or is it just a lottery on that side?   MV:  The engines are exactly the same. Everything is the same, so there is no excuse.    Q: The software or driver?   MV:  It's all the same.    ENDS     FIA Formula One World Championship    Formula 1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026Formula 100 Saturday, October 10, 2026 - 5:47pm  Saturday, October 10, 2026 - 5:47pm

title: F1 - 2026 Singapore Grand Prix Post-Sprint Press Conference Transcript
summary: Sport news  DRIVERS   1 – Max VERSTAPPEN (Red Bull Racing)    2 – Lewis HAMILTON (Ferrari)   3 – Charles LECLERC (Ferrari)     TRACK INTERVIEWS   (Conducted by David Coulthard)     Q: Charles, well, the heavens opened, you all had to be reactive. It looked like you had good pace there at the beginning of that Sprint race and then you were struggling towards the end. I assume the tyres were giving you some difficulty but put us in the cockpit.   Charles LECLERC:  Yeah, I mean, I struggled a lot from mid-race onwards. I went towards quite an aggressive balance, on the other side of what I normally do, with quite a weak front, which was quite good for the first part of the race. But then when it dried up, I was nowhere. So it was kind of tricky at the end.    Q: Yeah, well, you held on. We had the battle between the two McLarens who were hounding you at the end there. Did you see the coming together in your mirrors and breathe a sigh of relief?   CL:  I knew I had to have a very good exit out of five because I was very weak in all right-hand corners, particularly with the front left. And I had quite a good exit, but then I checked in my mirrors and I saw red lights of the back cars of the McLarens. So, I knew that something happened. And Kimi was also very strong towards the end. So yeah, just didn't have the pace at the end.    Q: OK, well, let me give to you your reward for finishing third in the Sprint. Charles Leclerc, congratulations. If you would like to stay here, please. Lewis Hamilton, great start to that Sprint. You had to make a decision very quickly whether to go left or right of the car in front. You made the right decision, and you were hounding the back of Max a lot at the start of that race. And then it looked a little bit like maybe with Charles, your tyres were fading towards the end.   Lewis HAMILTON:  Yeah, I mean, I had a mega start, which is awesome. I love driving this track in the rain and those conditions. So as soon as the heavens opened, I was like, "This is a great day." And then, yeah, I was trying to get close to him without killing my tyres. So, I wasn't really pushing that much, but I was bringing him in. And then I just realised that at this point, we've still got a long way to go. I don't think we'll be able to overtake in these conditions. There's only one line. And I backed off, and then the front right started to overheat a little bit. But then I got the controls back sorted, and then towards the end I started to push and started to close the gap. But, you know, it's a tough track to overtake.    Q: Absolutely. What are the learnings you take away from this Sprint, second place going into qualifying later?   LH:  Well, I think, I mean, we showed that we obviously have a good car. I think if we can do slightly better in qualifying, get both cars up there, I think we'll be able to really apply pressure tomorrow to both the Mercedes and the Red Bull. So, they are quick, of course, but we can be there hounding them. So hopefully we can position the car in a slightly better position in this qualifying session coming up. And yeah, also got a great crowd already, just on a Saturday. So big up to everyone here in Singapore.    Q: Lewis, congratulations. Let me please give to you your reward for your Sprint second place. And again, if you would like to just stay here. And we'll now hear from our Sprint race winner and a man that has now won on every circuit that he's competed in Formula 1. Max Verstappen, congratulations. That's back-to-back weekends when you've lost the start and then managed to come back again. You had a grandstand seat, first of all, for George getting a little bit wide out of the final corner and then managed the race perfectly to pick up those vital eight points.   Max VERSTAPPEN:  Yeah, I mean, the start was horrendous again. So that's definitely something that we need to improve on because if you have something like that tomorrow, that's your race over if nothing crazy happens. So yeah, not ideal. But then we got, of course, a bit lucky with what happened with George out of the last corner. And after that, you just want to keep it calm and under control because you know that you can't pass around here, and especially, I think, in a condition like this with the intermediates. So, we just tried to bring it home. And of course, happy to win here in the Sprint, but I also know that I want to win tomorrow and not today.    Q: Yeah, absolutely. Grand Prix tomorrow, Grand Prix qualifying coming later. I guess we'll all be watching the clouds to try and see what sort of conditions we'll have there. But in terms of picking up a first place in the Sprint, you've now completed all the circuits in your winning ways. How does it feel to do that here in Singapore?   MV:  I want to win tomorrow. I don't see this as a win in terms of actually winning a Grand Prix, you know. So we need to have a good qualifying. It will be very close with a lot of cars, I think, and we just need to try and make sure, of course, we are the best one out of them. But it will be, yeah, hopefully a good battle.    PRESS CONFERENCE      Q: Max, great job, very well done. How difficult was it to manage that race in those conditions?   MV:  Yeah, I mean, it was a bit weird, of course, in places where it was very wet and then in other places it was basically dry. So it's also just about managing the tyre till the end. You never, I guess, know what is the best way, but at the end of the day, I think the way we managed it was enough to win it. But at the same time, of course, when the tyres start wearing, as soon as you get onto a little bit of a damp patch, or because the rubber is, of course, falling off in some places, the corner actually becomes quite greasy because of the rubber. A tiny bit offline can cause you to go off or have a moment. So especially on a street circuit, you cannot afford to have too many moments. So it's just a management race till the end, but we, I think, managed it quite well.    Q: You looked inch-perfect out there. I mean, I suppose except for the start. Just talk us through what happened in the opening 200 metres or so.   MV:  Like always, it just doesn't go off the line. Yep, it just doesn't. We don't accelerate off the line.    Q: OK, well, look, you've been the class of the field so far this weekend. How confident are you for quali and the Grand Prix itself?   MV:  Well, I'm excited for qualifying, for sure. I want to, of course, try and fight for pole again, even though I do think that it will be a tight battle with a lot of cars, which I think is great, of course. And yeah, hope we can be in that fight. But still, we need to, of course, still do a start afterwards, and up until now we always have terrible starts. So yeah, we need to really understand what we're doing wrong there.    Q: Thank you very much. Very well done to you. Lewis, let's come to you. Great progress from you in the Sprint, and a huge amount of that work was done at the start. Just talk us through what happened there.   LH:  Yeah, congrats to Max. Yeah, I had a really good start. The grip was, on the formation lap when we pulled away, I felt like there was a lot of grip. So I decided to change my procedure for the main start, and as the lights were on, I was like, "I don't know if this is going to work." And then it did. So, I got a mega pull-away, chose the inside line, and everyone seemed to be braking early. So, it was pretty straightforward. And after, I had really good pace, holding on to Max, but there's basically one line here, and so overtaking is very, very difficult. And yeah, also to overtake the most powerful engine on the grid is not so easy either. So yeah, I just had to consolidate and hold on to second.    Q: And how difficult was it to keep the tyres alive for the full 20 laps?   LH:  The first part was relatively easy, and I was just managing behind Max. But then through the middle sector, it was completely dry. I probably pushed a little bit more than Max through that section, and then the right started to grain a little bit. And so then I had to pull back, and that's where Max extended that gap. And then I made some adjustments to the setup on the steering wheel and then managed the last few laps. I started to close the gap to him a little bit. But yeah, I'm just really happy to have recovered from what was a bad qualifying yesterday. And I hope that we can make the right changes so that we can be more competitive in the next session.    Q: Well, how much potential does the car have?   LH:  I think we have the potential to fight with Max for the front row at least. I mean, whether or not we can actually be ahead of them, we shall see. But I think the car is good here, and it's just really, you need to nail that, you need to get the setup right. And I think we were quite out of bed at the start of FP1. Normally, when we start practice, we usually have a car in a good place, but it wasn't in a good place. We had to then make lots of changes, and then it's a bit of just rolling the dice. And I think we were just massively overbalanced in qualifying. But I think we've learned from that, and I hope that, as I said, going into qualifying, we should be in a nice place.    Q: OK, very well done to you. Thank you, Lewis. And Charles, let's come to you now. You said a moment ago that it wasn't so easy for you out there. Just what were the main issues?   CL:  Probably opposite to what Lewis had. I think we had quite different cars, and yesterday for me that was quite positive, but today I struggled massively. I mean, front tyres, I had no fronts from lap 10 onwards and just struggled a lot to find any rotation anywhere on track. And so unfortunately, I was trying to save, but even by saving, I was just putting way too much energy in the front tyres. So, I just struggled quite a lot towards the end.    Q: What does that mean going forward for qualifying if it's on a dry racetrack?   CL:  If it's on a dry racetrack, I'm not going to change the car too much. I think some fine-tuning here and there. I know where to improve it on the dry. If it's wet, then we'll have to take a decision, and yeah, quite a big one.    QUESTIONS FROM THE FLOOR     Q: (Adam Cooper – AdamCooperF1) For all three of you, bearing in mind what happened to George, how tricky was that first lap? How aware were you of trying to stay off the kerbs? And for Lewis and Charles, how sketchy was it when George was coming back across the track and obviously you had to decide where to go? Max, if we could start with you, please.   MV:  Yeah, I mean, he was sideways already a few times in that first lap, so I think he was just pushing quite hard on the first lap already. And then in the last corner, he clipped the white line, and then, of course, it did send him left into the wall. Easy mistake to make, I guess. I'm lucky at the same time. But yeah, as soon as I saw him go, probably I was in the nicest position compared to the cars behind, because the spray, it's sometimes really hard to see what's going on.    Q: Lewis, can we just get your take on George's crash and how sketchy was it as he was coming back across the track?   LH:  I mean, it was pretty... I thought the grip was, it was like the highest grip, I would say, for the wet, for inters. You know, there's a lot of tracks where there's a lot less grip. But I mean, of course, if you touch the kerb or touch the white lines, it could be quite sketchy. I think the last corner, definitely I had a couple of snaps there, so it's so easy to do. And it wasn't in my way, so fine.    Q: Charles?   CL:  Yeah, it was a bit more sketchy for me because George started to then reverse in the middle of the straight, but then stopped. And yeah, with the visibility as well as with the half SM open, I mean, we have the front SM in that part of the track, it's always quite tricky. But yes, everything was fine. Just the visibility was quite poor, particularly on this part of the track.    Q: (Ronald Vording – Motorsport.com) So a question to Max. You've said a couple of times before you feel no emotional satisfaction or whatever from winning a Sprint, but is this different in any way given the Red Bull struggles in Singapore in the past? And on the start, is it basically still hit and miss, or based on today and Kuala Lumpur, do you have some ideas what you want to try for tomorrow?   MV:  Emotion is the same. It doesn't matter if you have won or not at the track before. And with the start, we have a few limitations that we have to work on. And probably also from our side, I think we have to do a better job, because Racing Bulls sometimes do start better than us. So, we just need to be better.    Q: (Dzhastina Golopolosova – F1Maximaal.nl)  Question to Max. Max, there was so much drama going on behind you in the race with all these incidents and retirements. What was the race like from your perspective? And was it actually quite calm at the front, or was there more going on than we could see?  MV:  It was calm in a way, but at the same time you need to be focused. You know, it's easy, like if you relax, to make a mistake or go wide. It was more just paying attention and staying calm, but paying attention to the road ahead of you with your tyres degrading. Yeah, the road, of course, becoming dry in some places but greasy in others, and you just have to be patient.    Q: (Tom Westbrook – Reuters) Just wondering, to all three of you, what sort of a future do you think Singapore has as a Sprint race venue, given how difficult overtaking can be here?   LH:  I don't know. I mean, I love the race here. I really do love the race. I was just saying to Max, I think they need to change the track to maybe a longer straight somewhere in order to allow us to, for it to be truly a great racing circuit. Because I think it has the potential to be a great racing circuit. It's a great track to drive over a single lap in qualifying, but there literally just isn't many... There's like one place, I guess, really, that you could potentially get close to overtake. But then in other places, like 16, the crest in the middle of the track, sparks come up because the track isn't particularly flat. I don't know if it's for the rain or whatever it is, but I think there's some adjustments that can be made to make this 100% a great circuit. But whether they're going to do that, I don't know. But I thought it was fun. But if it was dry, that would have been probably the most boring race for you to have watched. It was the wet, the rain, that made it exciting. So, if you can always make it rain, then it's always going to be a great Sprint race. But otherwise, it would probably just have been straightforward tyre management, everyone sticking behind each other.  MV:  I mean, yeah, I think we shouldn't host a Sprint where you can't pass. You know, you have tracks where you can race and can overtake, but of course, in some places you cannot pass, and we are going to have Sprints there also next year. Yeah, I mean, I'm fine. I mean, I just do my thing and then that's it, right? But yeah, it's not what I like. The track is great, but also the problem we have at the moment is with the Overtake Mode, it barely does anything here. You don't really gain a lot on the straights. So also that, with how all the rules are at the moment, with our lovely batteries, yeah, it just doesn't do much. You can't even get super close or have a massive overspeed at the moment. So I, of course, fully agree we need to have a longer straight or more of a proper hairpin to overtake. But even with that, also we need a bigger delta on the straight.  CL:  I agree. I don't think it makes sense to have any Sprint races on city tracks in general. And we probably should use these Sprints to have them on tracks where it's easy to overtake, where you can have a lot of racing action and it actually adds something to the weekend. Whereas here or Monaco, I don't think it adds anything to the weekend.    ENDS     FIA Formula One World Championship    Formula 1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026Formula 100 Saturday, October 10, 2026 - 1:29pm  Saturday, October 10, 2026 - 1:29pm

title: F1 – Verstappen wins rain-affected Singapore Sprint as Russell crashes out and McLaren pair collide
summary: Sport news Max Verstappen claimed victory in a dramatic, rain-affected Sprint at the 2026 FIA Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix, as Mercedes’ George Russell crashed out of the lead on the opening lap and a late collision between McLaren team-mates Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris reshuffled the order.  The Red Bull driver crossed the line 2.591 seconds ahead of Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, with Charles Leclerc completing the podium despite struggling with deteriorating intermediate tyres in the closing stages. Championship leader Kimi Antonelli finished fourth for Mercedes.  Heavy rain swept across the Marina Bay Street Circuit shortly before the scheduled start, leaving standing water at Turns 2 and 3 and forcing a 30-minute delay. With conditions varying considerably between sectors, the field completed two formation laps before starting the 20-lap contest on intermediate tyres.  When racing began, Russell made a stronger getaway than polesitter Verstappen and seized the lead into Turn 1. Hamilton also enjoyed an excellent start, climbing from sixth to third ahead of Leclerc, Piastri and Norris.  However, Russell’s advantage disappeared at the end of the opening lap when the Mercedes driver lost control over the kerb exiting the final corner and crashed into the inside barrier.  Verstappen inherited the lead, while further incidents added to the opening-lap drama. Lance Stroll and Sergio Pérez collided at Turn 16, eliminating both drivers, while Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar retired after reporting an engine-braking problem.  The Safety Car was deployed as marshals recovered the stranded cars. During the neutralisation, Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad spun before rejoining at the back, while Alpine’s Franco Colapinto retired with a technical problem.  Racing resumed after five laps behind the Safety Car, with Verstappen controlling the restart ahead of Hamilton and Leclerc. Behind them, Haas driver Oliver Bearman overtook Pierre Gasly following a prolonged wheel-to-wheel battle through the opening sector.  Gasly subsequently lost further ground, including a position to Nico Hülkenberg. The Alpine driver complained that the Audi had forced him wide, but the stewards decided no further investigation was necessary.  At the front, Hamilton initially remained within striking distance of Verstappen, the gap fluctuating between seven tenths and 1.4 seconds through lap 11.  However, as the circuit continued to dry, managing the increasingly worn intermediate tyres became crucial. Verstappen gradually extended his advantage, opening a three-second margin by lap 13 and stretching it to five seconds three laps later.  Leclerc, meanwhile, struggled increasingly with front-tyre degradation and came under pressure from the McLarens and Antonelli. With three laps remaining, Piastri and Norris had closed onto the Ferrari’s tail, setting up a tense conclusion.  On the final lap, Norris attempted to pass Piastri at Turn 5, but the McLaren pair made contact and spun. Norris dropped to eighth, while Piastri failed to complete the final lap, although he was classified 14th. Their collision allowed Antonelli to secure fourth ahead of Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson, Bearman and Hülkenberg.  Verstappen, meanwhile, maintained control to take the chequered flag ahead of Hamilton, with Leclerc holding on to third by just 0.367 seconds from Antonelli.  Gasly and Esteban Ocon completed the top 10, followed by Fernando Alonso, Carlos Sainz and Lindblad. title: F1 – Verstappen seals pole for Singapore Sprint ahead of Russell and Leclerc
summary: Sport news Max Verstappen took top spot in Sprint Qualifying for the 2026 FIA Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix, beating Mercedes’ George Russell by 0.120 seconds as Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc finished third at the Marina Bay Street Circuit.  The Red Bull driver posted a lap of 1:31.156 in the final segment to secure first place ahead of Saturday’s Sprint, following a closely contested qualifying session. However, his result remained subject to a stewards’ investigation into an alleged yellow flag infringement during SQ1.  Leclerc finished 0.243 seconds behind Verstappen, with Oscar Piastri fourth for McLaren, just 0.055 seconds adrift of the Ferrari driver. Lando Norris took fifth ahead of Lewis Hamilton, while championship leader Kimi Antonelli qualified seventh. Liam Lawson was eighth, with Isack Hadjar and Pierre Gasly completing the top 10 after having their SQ3 lap times deleted.  The opening segment was interrupted when Sergio Pérez hit the barriers and damaged his Cadillac’s front wing. As he attempted to return to the pits, debris was left on the circuit and the session was red flagged with six minutes remaining.  Only a handful of drivers had completed representative laps before the stoppage, with Hamilton leading on 1:33.748. Verstappen’s apparent pass on the Ferrari under yellow flags was subsequently referred to the stewards for investigation after the session.  With limited time available following the restart, the closing minutes brought a succession of improvements as drivers sought to secure places among the leading 16.  Verstappen eventually set the quickest time, a 1:33.477, to finish 0.018 seconds ahead of Leclerc. Russell was third, followed by Hamilton and Audi’s Nico Hülkenberg. Hadjar, Norris and Piastri also progressed, with the latter recovering after abandoning his first attempt.  Arvid Lindblad missed the cut in 17th place, ahead of Aston Martin’s Lance Stroll. Alexander Albon was 19th for Williams, followed by Pérez and Valtteri Bottas in the two Cadillacs. Carlos Sainz finished last in the second Williams.  Verstappen established the initial SQ2 benchmark on the mandatory Medium tyres with a lap of 1:32.724. Ferrari then moved ahead, Hamilton improving on the Red Bull driver’s effort before Leclerc lowered the target to 1:32.457.  Russell faced a more difficult passage through the second segment. A lock-up at Turn 13 compromised an attempt to improve, and gains from Hadjar and Alpine’s Franco Colapinto subsequently pushed him outside the top 10.  The Mercedes driver responded on his final run, climbing to fourth and displacing Colapinto, who ended the session 11th. Hülkenberg was eliminated in 12th, ahead of Oliver Bearman, Gabriel Bortoleto, Fernando Alonso and Esteban Ocon.  With Soft tyres required for the eight-minute final segment, McLaren and Mercedes headed out first. Norris set the early pace with a 1:31.587, ahead of Piastri, while Russell and Antonelli initially trailed the McLaren pair.  Leclerc then edged ahead by 0.019 seconds with a lap of 1:31.568. Hamilton was competitive through the opening sector but lost time later in the lap, recording a 1:31.702 that would leave him sixth.  Leclerc subsequently improved to 1:31.399, but Verstappen’s sole SQ3 attempt proved decisive. A strong opening sector laid the foundations for the Dutchman to move clear, with his advantage maintained through the remainder of the lap.  Russell’s late improvement to 1:31.276 secured second place, splitting Verstappen and Leclerc. Piastri also improved, taking fourth with a 1:31.454, while Norris retained fifth on his earlier effort.  Behind Hamilton, Antonelli’s 1:31.849 left the championship leader 0.693 seconds off the fastest time. Lawson completed the timed runners in eighth with a 1:32.341, while deleted laps left Hadjar and Gasly without times in the final segment, placing them ninth and 10th respectively for Saturday’s Sprint.   2026 FIA Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix – Sprint Qualifying  1 Max Verstappen Red Bull/Red Bull Ford 11: 31.156 - - 2 George Russell Mercedes 1'31.276 0.120  3 Charles Leclerc Ferrari 1'31.399 0.243  4 Oscar Piastri McLaren/Mercedes 1'31.454 0.298  5 Lando Norris McLaren/Mercedes 1'31.587 0.431  6 Lewis Hamilton Ferrari 1'31.702 0.546  7 Kimi Antonelli Mercedes 1'31.849 0.693  8 Liam Lawson Racing Bulls/Red Bull Ford 1'32.341 1.185  9 Isack Hadjar Red Bull/Red Bull Ford - - - 10 Pierre Gasly Alpine/Mercedes - - - 11 Franco Colapinto Alpine/Mercedes 1'33.249 2.093  12 Nico Hülkenberg Audi 1'33.420 2.264  13 Oliver Bearman Haas/Ferrari 1'33.423 2.267  14 Gabriel Bortoleto Audi 1'33.466 2.310  15 Fernando Alonso Aston Martin/Honda 1'33.734 2.578  16 Esteban Ocon Haas/Ferrari 1'34.368 3.212  17 Arvid Lindblad Racing Bulls/Red Bull Ford 1'35.136 3.980  18 Lance Stroll Aston Martin/Honda 1'35.662 4.506  19 Alexander Albon Williams/Mercedes 1'36.130 4.974  20 Sergio Pérez Cadillac/Ferrari 1'36.760 5.604  21 Valtteri Bottas Cadillac/Ferrari 1'36.868 5.712  22 Carlos Sainz Williams/Mercedes 1'37.376 6.220     FIA Formula One World Championship    F1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026F101 Friday, October 9, 2026 - 4:56pm  Friday, October 9, 2026 - 4:56pm

title: F1 - 2026 Singapore Grand Prix - Friday Press Conference Transcript
summary: Sport news  TEAM REPRESENTATIVES  -  Alan PERMANE (Racing Bulls), Zak BROWN (McLaren), Toto WOLFF (Mercedes)     Q: Toto, if we could start with you, please. Let's begin with upgrades. They proved frustrating last time out at Sepang. Kimi is continuing to use them here. What did you learn? Did you learn any more about them in FP1?   Toto WOLFF:  Good afternoon, everyone. The complication is that we've brought a big upgrade to Baku, and Baku is so tricky and a little bit of an outlier in terms of the temperatures that we've seen on Friday and Saturday, and with the tarmac being broken, or the tarmac being quite open, that we kind of didn't know whether the upgrade wasn't working as we thought or whether it was influenced indeed by the track conditions. And that's why we decided to go to Singapore, have two different specs of cars and see what it’s going to do, well knowing that Singapore is an outlier of a track too. So, we've done that exercise in FP1. There is a pattern, but most importantly is to really dissect what's working and what's not on the old and the new spec and then finding a way forward, picking the best bits and seeing where the development direction needs to get us in order to extract the optimum lap time. Now, having said that, obviously running two different cars is not always ideal, but it's a compromise we just need to take. So, we have two test pilots at the moment. We need to take it in order to assure that we're doing the right thing for next year as well.    Q: You say there's a pattern. Is the pattern similar to what you were seeing at Sepang?   TW:  Yeah, there is a similar pattern, that the new car seems to be a little more tricky to drive. Not saying it's necessarily slower, because there will be goodness in it, but maybe we haven't just found a way of putting it all together and tuning it. The older car is a bit more stable, grippy, but that is really just one data point. That is one free practice session, and it will be needing more time to really come to more conclusive information.    Q: And with the 2027 car beginning to take shape back in the factory, how crucial is it to find a way forward with this upgrade?   TW:  Very. I mean, we've put a few months of upgrades into the car, clearly pointing in a direction that we think is advantageous, and maybe we just need to calibrate it a little bit in order to find the right way forward for 2027.    Q: OK, quick word on drivers now. There's been some speculation in the media about some of the decisions that have been made between your two drivers this year. What would you say to those people who feel that the team has favoured Kimi at times?   TW:  They're brainless, whoever thinks that. I mean, it's completely nonsensical. We've had it in the past with Lewis fans. I mean, literally, I don't know what's going on. Do they think I have a button that says, "George engine failure now", or disadvantaging one driver against the other when we are fighting for a Constructors' Championship, when we have always had the mindset of providing everybody equal material? But I guess this is maybe where social media goes today. People hide behind their screens and then they lash out. There's a lot of polarisation going on, and sometimes I read what people write. I find it hilarious. These people really contribute to my own entertainment when they are abusing the team or myself. I'm Satan, I've heard. So, yeah, overall funny.  Zak BROWN:  Silver Arrows rules will fix it. I’ve got a book I can share with you.  TW:  Yeah. You obviously… You have the exclusive rights on fruits, Papaya Rules, so we need to come up with something better. But really zero understanding and respect for people who come up with these things. They should, rather than watching Formula 1, they should do Teletubbies or some Mickey Mouse.    Q: All right, Toto, thank you for that. Zak, if we could come to you now. The last couple of races have been difficult for the team. With seven races to go, look, what's the target between now and the end of 2026?   ZB:  The target is to come into every race weekend with a chance to win. We look better here in Free Practice 1. We feel more on top of things than we have the last couple of races, and then, of course, won a couple of races prior to that. So, I think it shows how competitive the sport is and how quickly the top four teams, and the whole grid for that matter, everyone's kind of moving around in levels of competitiveness. But our goal is to try and come to each race weekend and win, but that's easier said than done.    Q: And when you look at the final standings, if, for example, you finish in the top three, how would you rate your season?   ZB:  Difficult. A lot of progress, lots of learning. Again, I think if you go to Australia, everyone thought Merc's going to win 24 races on the trot, and they've had an unbelievable season. I'd be very surprised if they didn't win the championship. But knowing them as I do, that's not going to be the attitude any race team has, right? It's not over until it's over. But now you've got four teams that have won races. I think you have four teams that can come into this weekend and win. And so here we are again with an unbelievably competitive Formula 1. You've had Alpine with a pole, and when you look at the timing screens, whether it's a Racing Bulls or an Alpine, no one's far away. So, it's getting closer and closer. So, this has been a tough year, a learning year, but I want to finish on a high note so we can go into '27 fighting for the championship.    Q: What about the drivers? In here yesterday, Lando was talking about the way he's driven, how pleased he is with some of the performances he's put in. How have you seen him kick on as a world champion?   ZB:  He's just getting better and better. Very confident. You can see when we have a bad day at the office, his approach to the next session is like a world champion. He shrugs it off quickly. I think we've all seen at times he can be too critical of himself over the years, and now I think he's got that world champion confidence where it's like, "Well, let's get it next session." So I've not seen him ever drive this well, as is, but he's still the same Lando, which I think is great. So, he's changed on track in a world champion way, but he's still the Lando I think we all know and love off the track.    Q: What about Oscar? He seems to have struggled more with the car, got better in the last couple of races. Is he back to the Oscar you know?   ZB:  Yeah, I think he is. And I think we've seen with these cars, it's kind of mixed up the field a little bit, right? Lewis is getting the better out of the Ferrari right now. George got more out of the car last year than Kimi. That's moved around. I think these cars are so complex. I think some have kind of adapted a little bit quicker than others, but I'm liking everything I see out of Oscar. I think he's feeling much more confident, on top of things. I like where both our drivers are now.    Q: OK, Zak, thank you for that. Alan, we'll come to you now. Can we start by talking about Arvid in FP1? First time he's been to this track in Singapore. Just how has he settled in with just that one practice session?   Alan PERMANE:  Yeah, pretty well. I did the same trick with him here as I did in Montreal. New track, Sprint weekend. I just said to take the FP1, Sprint Qualifying and Sprint like FP1, FP2, FP3. So, no pressure. We don't expect you to be top 10 in FP1. And it seems to work, that approach. It definitely takes the pressure off him and just allows him to drive and get on with it. So, a very decent session. We didn't have the best car to start with this morning. Not this morning, is it? This evening, this afternoon, wherever we are. And had to make some changes to both cars in the middle of that session. So, we were running around quite close to the back for that first run on Hards. Made a decent change to both and figured out we had some issues. Much more comfortable then, and then onto the Mediums at the end, we looked to be in our normal sort of place.    Q: While we're talking drivers, most teams have confirmed their line-ups for 2027. VCARB hasn't. When can we expect news?   AP:  I don't want to give you a definite date. You know, no, that's not going to work. It's going to be in the coming weeks, let's say. I mean, we're in no rush. I think everyone knows we've got two fantastic drivers. We've got a fantastic driver in F2 at the moment, and they're all there and ready to go. But three doesn't fit into two, of course, and we're just going to take a little bit more time and make sure we get the right pairing for next year.    Q: What's the key criteria for you?   AP:  There's many, many, many things. I guess top of the list is speed and pace and all that goes with that. But there's lots, of course, in the background because we're in a slightly unique situation, I guess. We want to bring on young drivers, we want to bring on young talent, and of course we have one eye on them progressing in the future. So, it's not just about the here and now, it's also about what they can do in the future.    QUESTIONS FROM THE FLOOR     Q: (Nelson Valkenburg – Viaplay) I have a question for you, Toto and Zak. James Vowles has been quite active in pushing some changes for the cost cap, and he seems to be making some headway in terms of getting support in the paddock. Do you agree that the cost cap needs changes? And as top teams, do you agree with what he's proposing as a sliding scale based on points scored? Would you support it?   TW:  Well, there are a few topics. The reason the cost cap came in was in order to balance the performances between small teams and bigger teams. We had to actually quite dramatically restructure, whilst other teams were below the cap and they were able to hire. So, I think that was the main idea. Now, where the cost cap has taken us is that obviously we have profitable entities, and that is, from a pure economic effect, nice. But it's also suppressing salaries. We were always an aspirational sport. We attracted the best talent from the best universities because of the possibilities you had in Formula 1. Now you can get someone into a Formula 1 team today on enthusiasm, but at a certain stage, when after five, six or seven years and you have a PhD, your salaries are still depressed versus a tech company or a hedge fund or investment banking, that becomes a problem. So, where we stand, I'd love to have a little bit more room in the cost cap for lower salaries, a bracket, rather than buying new front wings, but give the possibility of paying a little bit more and being attractive as a sport. Now, I'm not sure that many find this a good idea. Obviously, it also depends on the size of the team. I think we exchanged that is something we would like to do, but if you have the reality of the budget, a smaller team is not going to be happy about us having five million more in the cost cap to spend for PhDs. So that's the second point. The third point is that what James is alluding to is the CapEx allowance or the CapEx possibilities. Now, how the regs were changed was that rather than having this CapEx budget, your CapEx would go into operational costs, into OpEx. So, the consequence is the teams that spent a lot in the past on CapEx, like us, for example, have a huge amount of costs that we need to depreciate in the cost cap. The ones that haven't spent a lot obviously have much more possibility to spend on infrastructure or whatever you want to, what was CapEx before. So I think I have super sympathy with a team like Williams and with James, and he's super clever, but we just need to find the right balance of not undoing something that we actually consciously changed a year or two ago. So, yeah, it's just a forward-moving discussion. Personally, I don't like the concept of adjustment based on some positions. BoP for me is like a red mist. We're having these tiny little adjustments on aero time, ATR, which is almost invisible to the spectator and hasn't been a big thing because it's really tiny. We have the catch-up mechanisms on the power units. If someone were to fall behind dramatically, then you get that opportunity, but it wasn't a leapfrogging mechanism. So, the job that the FIA have done in that respect I think is very good. They haven't allowed any politics to creep in, people making noises that they wanted to do or not. I think they handled that very well. So, do we really want another mechanism where you're being allowed to have more CapEx, OpEx based on your championship position? I'm not sure.  ZB:  Yeah, I think we do a good job as a sport of reviewing financial regulations, sporting regulations, technical regulations. And I think we all collectively work well together to always try and move forward. Sport is very complex. I think the biggest difference in racing teams are the people, the culture. I know we don't have the largest infrastructure in Formula 1. I don't think we have the second or third largest infrastructure in Formula 1. We've got a customer engine, all these things which you hear over the years you can't win a championship with, and we have. And I think that's because we're a really well-performing team of people. So always open-minded. I do think we made a step forward in combining the CapEx and the OpEx. So now you have a decision to make where to invest, just like you have a decision to make on what drivers you want to bring on board. So, I think it's complicated, always open-minded. But I think if you look last year, it was the closest grid in the history of Formula 1. And then when I was growing up racing, most of the time it was one or two teams winning. Now it's four. Fifth got a pole this year. So, I think the sport's extremely competitive as it is, but always open to any conversation.  TW:  I think, can I add to this? You are a good example. McLaren is a very good example. A team that wasn't owned by a big mothership that had endless funding like some of us, but able to work yourself out of a situation that wasn't good, starting to win races two years ago and then finally winning a championship.  ZB:  Two.  TW:  Sorry, two, of course!  ZB:  It was hard, so I don't want to forget the second one.  TW:  Yeah, that was a hard one. Yeah. So, good example. And then when you look at the pecking order today, you have VCARB that is always there or thereabouts in the top 10, performing. You have Alpine, you've seen they made a big step forward, and then there are four of us bigger teams that, like Zak said, four of us have won races. So I think overall, as an organisation, and I know that James is carrying with him huge ballast with an old-school, old-style Formula 1 team with massive machine shops and lots of production and making it leaner and more efficient and convincing people that the structure in the future needs to be different is super difficult. But I don't think that the CapEx/OpEx is going to unleash much more potential, in my opinion, and not with an adjustment mechanism.    Q: (Craig Slater – Sky Sports) Question for Toto. Just picking up on what you said earlier, Toto. Clearly, it's ridiculous to talk about bias, but it's an old thought within Formula 1 that a team would naturally gravitate towards the driver delivering results, which obviously has been largely Kimi this year. How sensitive have you been as team boss to keep an eye on George's sort of psychology in that regard? And do these next two events, if you were to take a grid penalty in both, does it take the pressure off just a little bit to not have that direct comparison with Kimi? Do you sense this sort of regroup in that area?   TW:  I've always tried, since I came into Formula 1, even in my Williams days, to be the most balanced and the most structured, transparent, sorry, the most balanced and most transparent with the drivers. I have told this story before. I remember being a complete rookie and running into Alain Prost on the grid of a race, and I said, "Just out of interest, why did it go so wrong between you and Senna?" And he said, "Because we never knew what the team was about. You felt that you were the flavour of the month one time, and then two months later you thought the politics were going against you. There were different situations where you had the feeling that you're really not wanted." So, I took it as my challenge to keep it always balanced. And it was not easy with Lewis and Nico back in the day. And that's why people can think what they want, but the integrity in that respect is something that's important for me, and the drivers know it. We have had Kimi since he was 11. He is an integral part of the team. It is very nice to see him grow, be in a position now that he is fighting for a championship at such a young age, the talent he has. And then on the other side, George, who has been with us since he was 17, someone that I feel a lot of, how can I say, emotions for and compassion. We are very close. We are spending time with Carmen and Susie off the track with each other. If people would see that we're travelling together, we're having coffee in the same coffee shop, we're going to the gym, that's why it's pretty annoying to have some lunatics that have no understanding really about how relationships work coming up with these kinds of accusations. So, I don't pay any attention to this. Most important is that George knows how the team is and Kimi knows, and we will always try to give them equal opportunity. And when it comes to the upgrade, it's a good example. We don't know which one is going to be quicker. And so you take a decision and say, "Let's try to find out." And there is no great political thinking behind it. And when it comes to racing, like the Papaya Rules, we have always been very clear that we're not standing in each other's way. We don't like the yo-yo racing that could cost a position if someone is close to us, and the quicker car, if it's behind, is always going to have an advantage. And that could go either direction, doesn't matter. Even if it is now that it's more realistic for Kimi to win a championship in sheer mathematical probability, we would still give George the same opportunities. And that's important. That's the ethos and the integrity on which the team has operated since 2013, since I came, and we are going to stick to that. And then people can think what they want.    Q: (Jon Noble – The Race) To Alan on the cost cap issue. Obviously Racing Bulls is a team outside of the top four and would in theory stand to benefit. Where do you stand on the debate and would you support the proposal if it goes to vote in the Commission?   AP:  I think both these guys had really good points, especially Zak saying about how close things were last year. And that isn't by accident. And I think that's linked to some of the things that Toto said about the aero rules, the wind tunnel rules, the ATR stuff. It just allows a little tweak. And of course, as you have longer regulation cycles, the teams close up and drivers close up, and I think that's definitely something we want. I don't think we would support a wholesale change to the cost cap rules to start being able to spend huge amounts more money because I think it's served us very well for the, I don't know how many years we're into it now, six years we're into it now. I think it's served Formula 1 very, very well. And I think maybe there are tweaks to do, for sure. But as Toto said, if you want to spend a whole lot of money on CapEx, you can. The mechanism's in there. So if James wants to go and spend $100 million on something, he can do that. You just pay it off over the X number of years. So, the mechanism is already there.    Q: (Christian Menath – Motorsport-Magazin.com) Question for you, Toto. You touched on it earlier with the doubts on the upgrade and what it means for 2027. Do you think this has always been the biggest risk of your strategy this year, with having one big upgrade, that you have no recalibration of the system and that you need the clarity for the development route in '27?   TW:  Yes, you have a point. I think that we are one of those large organisations that needs to be very careful how and when we spend our cost cap money. And we felt that the right strategic decision was to work towards a bigger one and then introduce it. Obviously, with the risk of if it doesn't work as you've anticipated, it's just quite difficult to dial yourself out and understand why it hasn't worked. So, it's something which we will look at in the future of saying maybe we'll do smaller steps, and then if there is a warning light saying, "OK", it's easier to undo. But there is no clear way at that stage because so far it has worked. I just remember 2022, which went well. We thought we had one and a half seconds we're putting on the car at the beginning of the season, and that backfired. But since then, this year particularly, every upgrade we brought on the car, remember Montreal was a big hit, a big hit in terms of it worked very well. So, if that didn't, why? That's the most important question. And if we come to conclusions that say this is what wasn't as expected, then we have to obviously think for the future.    Q: (Martin Moravecs – DPA) A question to Toto, please. You've been already talking about Nico and Lewis back then. At the end of the year, it will be 10 years ago that Nico was world champion and retired. How do you look back on this battle between Nico and Lewis, and how do you see him nowadays, Nico, as an entrepreneur or businessman?   TW:  I'll start with the second one. There are not many Formula 1 drivers, other than Niki, who I know that have been able to kind of reinvent themselves in a totally different career. And I see Nico a lot. I respect him a lot. We are friends. He set up a venture capital fund that is one of the best performing. He is giving it 24/7. He is very hard-working. He is respected within the tech industry very much. I am happy to be invested there and associated, and you really need to take your hat off, seeing what he's been able to achieve in this very short time of 10 years since he's left the sport. So that's the current situation. Looking back at it, I wish I would have had the 10 years more experience than I have today, because there's a few things I would have handled differently and maybe avoided some of the controversy, particularly in the last race where we tried to micromanage a situation that didn't need to be managed, in my opinion. And that was my fault. So yes, 10 years. It's crazy how fast time runs. It feels like it's maybe five years ago, but we've moved on from that. My relationship and the team's relationship with Lewis is as strong as it can be whilst being rivals on track, and the same with Nico.    ENDS      FIA Formula One World Championship    Formula 1   SEASON 2026  Sport  Circuit 1SportFIA Formula One World ChampionshipCircuitSEASON 2026Formula 100 Friday, October 9, 2026 - 1:41pm  Friday, October 9, 2026 - 1:41pm

title: F1 – Russell quickest in sole practice session for Singapore Grand Prix ahead of Leclerc and Norris
summary: Sport news George Russell set the fastest time in the sole free practice session for the 2026 FIA Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix, beating Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc by 0.198s as McLaren’s Lando Norris finished third.  The Mercedes driver posted a best lap of 1:32.274 on Soft tyres, with Norris 0.273s behind. Lewis Hamilton took fourth for Ferrari, ahead of Oscar Piastri, while Max Verstappen was sixth and quickest of those running the Medium compound.  With the Sprint format limiting practice to one hour, drivers headed out promptly when the session began at 16:30 local time. Track temperatures reached 53°C, giving teams conditions considerably warmer than those expected for Sprint Qualifying and the Grand Prix, both scheduled for night-time running.  Most drivers began on Hard tyres as they assessed grip around the dusty Marina Bay Street Circuit. Russell reported a stiff ride over the bumps, while Lance Stroll went into the escape road at Turn 1 and Norris ran off at Turn 16.  As the surface improved, Norris lowered the benchmark to 1:34.367 around the quarter-hour mark. Leclerc then became the first driver below 1:34 with a lap of 1:33.969, before Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli moved ahead with 1:33.830.  Norris subsequently took to the run-off at Turn 9 after a near miss with the barriers, but the session’s principal interruption came when Nico Hülkenberg stopped near the pit exit with approximately 20 minutes remaining.  The Audi driver reported a gearbox problem over the radio, prompting a brief Virtual Safety Car period while his car was moved back into the pit lane. Hülkenberg completed 16 laps, the fewest of any driver, and finished 18th.  Teams continued their longer runs before switching to performance laps during the closing stages. Russell was among the first to fit Soft tyres and immediately went quickest with 1:32.864. Piastri followed just 0.034s behind, while Leclerc abandoned his initial attempt after reporting traffic at Turn 5.  Hamilton briefly took first place with 1:32.821, but Russell improved to his session-winning time inside the final five minutes. Leclerc secured second with 1:32.472, ahead of Norris on 1:32.547.  Hamilton’s final improvement to 1:32.773 left him 0.499s adrift, with Piastri fifth on 1:32.838. Verstappen recorded 1:33.006 on Medium tyres, finishing 0.519s clear of Antonelli, who used the same compound and ran deep at Turn 16 on his final attempt.  Isack Hadjar placed eighth in the second Red Bull, followed by Alpine’s Pierre Gasly and Racing Bulls’ Liam Lawson, completing the top 10.  Oliver Bearman was 11th for Haas, ahead of Arvid Lindblad and Esteban Ocon. Fernando Alonso finished 14th, with Carlos Sainz 15th after completing a session-high 31 laps.  Gabriel Bortoleto headed Alexander Albon in 16th and 17th, while Franco Colapinto followed Hülkenberg in 19th.
